#10090. Staggering Scroll-Driven Animations with animation-range-start

The other day on the CSS-Tricks Slack channel, Danny Schwartz shared an interesting recent Master.dev article by Ashutosh Biswas on how to stagger CSS scrolling animations using a clever combo of several emergent CSS features and a lot of math, which Ashutosh admits is “a huge formula and can look intimidating.”

When Danny Slacked the link for the Frontend Masters article, he described it as “CSS on drugs.” Speaking of drugs, I am on heavy prescription painkillers while recovering from a serious injury, so that might not help my current comprehension skills. Nevertheless, after reading Ashutosh’s article a few times, here’s a meme showing how I’d feel using such an elaborate algorithm for something as mundane as staggering the animations of some characters as they scroll into view.

Don’t get me wrong. I know the complexity is because Ashutosh is going for a generic solution in which we can connect a “progress value to an animation, scroll progress, or any other input to drive the staggering.”

In fact, I can dream up a scenario in which this might be what we want: Imagine a CSS karaoke machine that displays a ball bouncing on text that incrementally highlights, based on the user’s progress through the vocals measured via speech recognition. Running that kind of animation “not as a collection of independently timed objects, but as a single predictable, holistic effect driven by one progress value” might be exactly what the doctor ordered. This would be true because the staggered animations could be interrelated, and the overall animation would be driven by a custom input that’s not built into the browser.

But unlike this hypothetical scenario, replacing the passage of time with scroll progress to control animations is already built into modern CSS. I contend that we’d need a better reason to roll our own implementation than the examples Ashutosh gives.

Ashutosh showcases a scroll-driven use case as “one of those ideal scenarios where the stagger formula shines.” But a red flag that we’re in danger of reinventing something we can get for free is that the spec for scroll-driven animations is cognizant that if we opt to base an animation on scroll progress rather than on time, then, as Ashutosh says, “the animation we are going to achieve is different from traditional ones because we don’t include time in our considerations.” This is no surprise to the creators of scroll timeline, and the MDN docs make Ashutosh’s point in different words when introducing scroll timeline.

The docs also point out that animation-delay is only meaningful when we are using the default time-based document timeline. Therefore, animation-delay does not affect scroll-driven animations. But this is why CSS introduced animation-range-start, which allows us to delay a scroll-driven animation relative to scroll progress and not time.

So, as esoteric and trippy as the math-heavy approach appears, that could be because we are doing something that should be simple in an unusual way.

Let’s see if I’m right by rewriting Ashutosh’s demo to remove reliance on custom CSS functions and use animation-range-start instead.

Ashutosh’s rework of Frontend Masters’ animated tally of donations in the site footer is a nifty, subtle use of scrollytelling that makes the user feel invested in revealing that number.

Sidenote: The only qualm I have about this use of scroll-driven animations for the donation tally is that it might be too subtle — if the user scrolls too quickly, the animated entrance of each digit might occur too quickly to notice. Therefore, the donation tally could be a good case study for comparing the merits of scroll-driven versus scroll-triggered animations as design options. However, that story will have to wait for another day, as the focus of this article is only to show that the staggered scrolling CSS animations can be greatly simplified.

In the video below, my eight-year-old narrates, as a reminder that simplicity is key to the web we’re choosing to leave to the next generation. He compares the complex math in the original demo source code with my animation-range-start fork. He shows the two versions working side by side, demonstrating that sometimes the only thing we lose by judiciously deleting complex code is a headache.

And for those using a Chromium-based browser, my fork of the Pen is below. You can peruse the CSS to see how it does away with the grand unified theory of staggered scrolling animations, and instead deals only with the problem at hand. Since I preserved the original functionality, you’ll need to scroll gradually to appreciate the staggered animations.

I once tackled a related problem with a mathematical formula in a previous article, which touched on how we can use sibling-index() to “increment animation-range-start to stagger the delay before characters fade in as the user scrolls.”

The truth is, if we refuse to fall into the coding trap of possibly abstracting the wrong thing, we can use one line of CSS to replace a formula that took 1.3k words in the Frontend Masters article for me to still not fully grasp:

The 2.5% increment for each sibling is because there are eight characters to stagger, and I wanted to choreograph the animations such that they are delayed in evenly-spaced increments till the last character makes its animated entrance when it reaches 30% of the containment range (10% + 20%).

It was inadvertently apt to describe the original post as “CSS on drugs.” Once you reinvent one built-in CSS feature, you can’t stop there. You find yourself having to recreate more stuff that CSS should be able to do by itself. Sure enough, even after we get through the custom formulas that make scroll timelines do what they already do, Ashutosh announces, “Unfortunately, we can’t use easing keywords or cubic-bezier() or linear() functions here. We are left on our own to create easing functions.”

We shouldn’t have to because, despite the word “timing” in the name of the animation-timing-function property, MDN is clear that “animation-timing-function has the same effect when creating CSS scroll-driven animations as it does for regular time-based animations.” I know from experience that scroll-driven animations work with animation-timing-function because I used scroll-driven animations with steps() to animate a sprite climbing a ladder in my CSS scrollytelling game.

The problem in the land of CSS on drugs is that after merging all the staggered animations into one, the easing applies to the entire master timeline rather than to each element. It’s not a flaw in CSS, but a logical consequence of the “holistic effect driven by one progress value.” Be careful what you wish for.

To be fair, over the years I have seen impressive results from developers reinventing things the browsers already do, usually because the reinvention gives us control we couldn’t obtain otherwise.

I mention this to show that reinventing something like scroll timelines isn’t an inherently bad idea if we know why we’re doing it. After all, scroll timelines are only a reinvention of what developers were doing for decades prior in JavaScript. Having said that, I believe my rewrite of the staggered scroll-driven tally demo shows that the original approach was overkill for that example. Do let me know in the comments if you see any advantage to the custom CSS functions version over using animation-range-start.

And yet the thought that stuck with me about the Frontend Masters post is that it opens the door to linking the progress of a CSS animation to any arbitrary input value that could be used in a conceptually similar way to scroll timelines.

This really appeals to me, because even when I first started writing about scroll timelines in 2024, I mentioned that “I would love to see other input controls that can manipulate animation timelines. Imagine text fields progressing animations as you fill them out.” Or how about an animation driven by how closely the new password you are typing matches a password scheme?

Sidenote: Adam Argyle’s Prop For That library, which Geoff recently wrote up, makes it more convenient than ever to expose validation information about a field via CSS custom properties.

I can add my hypothetical karaoke machine scenario to the wishlist of custom progress inputs for controlling animations. How about an animation driven by the user’s progress through a quiz or a shopping cart?

Custom animation timelines would open the door to all sorts of engaging user experiences—but the code Ashutosh has shared may be the closest we are likely to get to driving CSS animations using values other than time or scroll progress.

Let me know in the comments if you can think of other types of progress inputs that could drive CSS animations to create immersive, interactive experiences.

#10086. UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The UK is betting on domestic AI and cyber investment to reduce reliance on US tech — but security leaders question whether the funding is too fragmented and too late.

The UK has announced major investments in strengthening its cyber defenses, designed to stave off the rise of faster, more complex attacks enhanced by AI tools. In late October, the government unveiled a funding package of approximately $800 million to strengthen cyber defenses and AI security investments.

The move comes as Kanishka Narayan, the UK's minister of artificial intelligence, said in a speech last month that "it seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber-defenses will be breached." He cited the recent trend of misaligned models escaping containment, citing the OpenAI incident in June during which an agent hacked an Australian government health agency.

But the UK government is also pushing toward another, related goal: digital sovereignty. In his speech, Narayan emphasized the need to "build in Britain to keep the public safe in Britain" and become less dependent on foreign providers, which has become a common goal for some countries following the US government's export control order for Anthropic earlier this year.

Related:Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

"We want the world's leading companies investing here, but we will not accept dependence as the price of that investment," Narayan said.

But industry-watchers argue that government investment to strengthen cyber-defenses while also achieving greater sovereignty by encouraging homegrown tech might be difficult to do all at once.

Two turning points appear to have shifted government policy in the UK and Europe this year, both involving the same US company: Anthropic. The first came with the AI company's unveiling of Project Glasswing in April for its Mythos frontier model, which sparked concerns about a coming "vulnpocalypse" for enterprise security teams.

"It created an almighty whirlpool of conversations," says Tim Williams, CEO of London-based Quod Orbis, which specializes in continuous controls monitoring. "And then there were lots of concerns about what that meant, and everybody seemed to panic. I think that panic has settled down now."

But another event — the Trump administration's ban on foreign nationals using Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models has had a far more lasting effect. The ban didn't just impact overseas companies and government agencies; the export controls effectively forced Anthropic to pull all access to the two models for several weeks.

The implications of abruptly losing access to valuable — and perhaps critical — AI technology through a sudden change in US policy accelerated an already growing conversation about reducing dependency on American tech companies. A crucial part of the UK government's funding package is designed to fuel British AI startups and invest in home-grown companies.

Related:AIを活用したサイバー攻撃の増加を受け、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの緊急資金拠出を推進

It's a solid idea, but infosec professionals see two issues with that approach. First, the funding package is split up between a number of initiatives, with approximately £154 million of the £600 million total devoted to strengthening current cyber-defenses, for example.

"If you look at the amount that they're putting into it, is that enough? Is that significant?" Williams asks.

Secondly, the UK is already well behind the curve with fueling homegrown AI and cloud companies. Amir Khan, managing director at Wire, tells Dark Reading that there's been chronic under-investment in emerging technologies in the country, which has led to missed opportunities in the past.

"In the UK, we had DeepMind before it was sold to Google [in 2014]," Khan says. "Had they known the impact that DeepMind would have now, would they still have sold it, or doubled down on it? Who knows? But it's another example of a large organization that grew in the UK, leaving to go to the US."

In fact, due to that kind of ongoing tech emigration, Khan says you could argue that the last good thing to come out of the UK's technology industry was Cambridge Analytica — a company that became embroiled in a scandal involving Facebook.

Related:UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

Time and again, experts have argued that organizations can't counter AI-driven threats effectively without AI-enabled defenses. But that complicates matters for the UK, which is looking to achieve tech sovereignty in the aftermath of the Anthropic ban.

For one, in some part because of the issues outlined above, many of the major AI companies — OpenAI, Meta, SpaceXAI (now SpaceX Super Intelligence), and Palantir Technologies — are also based in the US. And while there are plenty of AI startups these days, those companies may not have the scale needed for national defense systems.

Additionally, there's also the cost component. Williams says many of Quod Orbis' customers are looking to reduce their dependency on a single vendor or provider, whether it's for cloud, software, AI, or other technologies. "There's no question that, in speaking to our clients, that concentrated risk is a concern for them," he says.

But moving from, for example, one cloud provider to four or five can be challenging, especially for mid-market organizations, he says. They may not have the budgets of large enterprises, and they probably rely more heavily on the commercial discounts that the cloud giants like AWS, Microsoft, and Google Cloud Platform provide. "If they're spreading that investment out across multiple cloud providers, that can become more expensive for them," Williams says.

Khan agrees and points to the recent example of France migrating off Windows for government workstations and moving to Linux. But leaving the Microsoft ecosystem will require France to add several more technologies from different vendors. "That, for me, defeats the purpose because you've essentially taken away one provider and pulled in six," he says. "That doesn't really give you the flexibility you want."

Khan argues the UK sometimes sets the wrong target for tech sovereignty. "We talk as though we have to build every chip, every cloud, and every application ourselves," he says. "As you can imagine, that's an enormous undertaking, and it doesn't really get to the heart of the issue. For me, the questions are, can we make our own decisions about the technology that we depend on? Can we operate it on our terms?"

The UK can retain such operational authority, he says, by choosing providers and vendors that build that kind of customer controls directly into their products and services; for example, Khan notes that Wire offers customers a private cloud option for the messaging platform that organizations can control and operate based within whatever country they're located.

Whichever providers or vendors the UK government chooses, officials should be asking several key questions before investing: who holds the encryption keys, who can interrupt the service, and how realistic is it to move off that technology?

In the meantime, the UK government will continue to focus on strengthening the country's cyber defenses through these investments and efforts like the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill currently. But Williams is unsure if they will be enough.

"It's a step in the right direction, absolutely," he says. "But is it the investment I would expect to see in terms of being really concerned about the threat to the UK?"

#10081. Cost per task: Using cheap classifiers to route across Gemini models and thinking levels

Per-token API prices keep falling, yet engineering bills for autonomous coding agents keep climbing. Price per million tokens isn't the metric that actually governs production economics anymore. The dominating metric is now cost per successful task: total spend across every loop iteration, tool call, retry and internal thinking pass divided by the number of tasks that pass verification.

When an agent calls a high-thinking reasoning configuration for every micro-decision in its harness, you're paying deep-reasoning prices for questions a lightweight configuration already answers accurately. To prevent this unnecessary overhead, consider adding a lightweight routing layer that can intercept routine decisions before they ever reach an expensive reasoning model.That is the premise behind wiring TypeSafe's Jev classifier in front of Google Antigravity's model calls. Rather than generating text token by token, Jev—a specialized structured-output classifier designed for high-throughput decision pipelines—evaluates structured classification primitives in a single forward pass: a Choice from a list, a numeric Score or a Noul, which returns a 0 to 1 probability for a binary statement.

For full disclosure, Google has no partnership with TypeSafe, and this article is not an endorsement of TypeSafe or its products. Jev is used here as one example of a lightweight classifier, and the same routing pattern can be built with other classifiers, including Google-native ones. The Getting started with discriminative models codelab, for example, runs the same kind of classifier on DiffusionGemma, Google DeepMind's open-weights model, in your own Google Cloud project.

We ran a 50-question, auto-graded, coding-agent benchmark against live Gemini and Jev APIs to test whether a near-free classifier can route each task to the cheapest model that still gets it right. Here's what we learned:

The naive way to ask Jev to route a coding task is a single broad Choice question: simple or complex. When we tested that first on 16 coding-agent tasks, Jev routed nearly everything to simple, even tasks requiring an LRU cache trace or modular exponentiation. TypeSafe's documentation warns against this exact anti-pattern. If a question weighs multiple factors or requires a meta-judgment, decompose it into an atomic check.

When we replaced the broad Choice question with one atomic Noul question, it fixed the separation immediately. The question was: does answering this require performing more than one sequential calculation, simulation step or logical deduction, rather than a single direct lookup, format check or one-step classification?

On those initial 16 tasks, Jev routed 13 of 16 in agreement with our hand-labeled difficulty on the first run and 14 of 16 on the second pass. Many engineering teams ask whether they even need a classifier API when they can write a zero-cost regex and prompt-length heuristic in Python, matching words like sequence, modulo and race condition or escalating any prompt over 35 words.

On the 16 development questions used to write those exact rules, the local heuristic scored 15 of 16, or 93.8%. To test whether that heuristic survived contact with realistic coding-agent traffic, we froze its code without changing a character and added 34 unseen held-out tasks across seven coding-agent buckets: fact extraction, schema validation, short classification, single-hop code checks, state simulation traces, math or logic chains and subtle language-semantics bugs.

On the 34 held-out questions, the frozen heuristic dropped 23.2 percentage points to 70.6%. Realistic simple tasks such as extracting a port from a Kubernetes YAML manifest, a file path from a unified git diff header or a line number from a Python traceback exceeded 35 words and triggered false escalations. Conversely, concise multi-step code traces such as mutable default arguments across calls, Python dictionary key hashing on {1: "a", True: "b", 1.0: "c"} and C short-circuit evaluation lacked the heuristic's hardcoded puzzle words and were falsely routed to the simple path. Jev classified all 34 unseen tasks with 100.0% agreement, 34 of 34, reaching 48 of 50, or 96.0%, across the full suite.

A common mistake when building a fast-path router is assuming that setting a low maxOutputTokens cap on a reasoning model will make it spend less on easy tasks. Our 50-question data shows why that assumption fails.

When we compared gemini-3.8-flash with maxOutputTokens=300 against gemini-3.8-flash with maxOutputTokens=4096 while leaving thinkingConfig at the API default, both configurations spent almost identical thinking tokens on the 27 tasks Jev labeled SIMPLE:

Note: Figures reflect single-run experimental measurements on a sample test suite; actual latencies, token counts, and billed costs will vary based on prompt length, context caching, and production load.

Capping the model's output at 300 tokens didn't save any money on easy tasks. The cap is only a ceiling, and easy answers never came close to it. On the easy tasks, the capped version actually cost slightly more than the uncapped one. All the cap did was break 7 of the 25 hard tasks. On six of them, the model ran out of room while still reasoning and never gave an answer. On the seventh, it squeezed its reasoning to fit, finished on time and got the answer wrong.

So a Jev router that sends easy tasks to the capped model and hard ones to normal Flash got all 50 right. It still cost slightly more than skipping the router and using normal Flash for everything, and it was slower. If your cheap option doesn't actually make the model think less on easy tasks, no router can save you money. Not even a perfect one that costs nothing.

The obvious way to spend less on thinking is to ask the model to think less. So we ran a second round of tests with two lighter options: Flash-Lite, which doesn't think at all by default, and Gemini 3.8 Flash with its thinking level set to low. We added those results to the same results file, matched question by question.

A note on timing. Most of the router's time per task is spent in Flash-Lite and Flash calls, which we measured in the same run and time window as the plain Flash baseline, so the speed comparison between them is fair. Jev's own decision is a small share of the total and comes from the first round. Speed comparisons against default Flash or Pro mix the two rounds, so read those as approximate.

Note: Figures reflect single-run experimental measurements on a sample test suite; actual latencies, token counts, and billed costs will vary based on prompt length, context caching, and production load.

The 7-bucket breakdown shows where gemini-3.5-flash-lite and the heuristic router missed tasks and how Router Jev: Flash-Lite to 3.8 LOW recovered 100% accuracy:

The strongest setup without a router was Gemini 3.8 Flash on low thinking. It solved all 50 tasks. That's the number a router had to beat.

The Jev router beat it. It sends every task to Flash-Lite first and escalates only what Jev flags as complex. It also solved all 50 tasks, and it can help reduce both cost and response time compared with running low thinking on everything. On prompts this short the cost difference per task is small, so for an interactive agent the shorter wait is the bigger benefit.

Why it works. On its own, Flash-Lite answered every simple task in half a second but missed 6 of the 25 hard ones. Jev flagged all 6 as complex with high confidence and escalated them. That brought its cost close to what a perfect router would achieve.

The keyword heuristic was cheaper, but only because it got things wrong. It sent 5 hard tasks to Flash-Lite, and 2 of them failed, for 48 of 50.

Escalating to a heavier setting didn't pay here. Routing hard tasks to Flash on default thinking was cheaper than running default thinking everywhere. It still cost more than running low thinking on everything, which already solved all 50. A heavier escalation target only makes sense when the low setting starts failing.

Limits: one run per setup, 50 prompts with hand-assigned difficulty and simple automatic grading.

Two things in our results only show up once you look past it.

Routing and caching pull in opposite directions. Our test prompts were short, standalone tasks, and on those the Jev router helped reduce both cost and response time. Real coding agents often look different. They send the same big block of context on every turn, such as a map of the repository and the tool definitions. Agent Platform Context Caching stores that block so you pay 75% to 90% less to resend it. The catch is that a cache belongs to one model. If your agent switches between Flash-Lite and Flash from turn to turn, it either keeps two caches or loses the discount. The practical split: route short, self-contained tasks like log parsing or schema checks, and keep long, context-heavy turns on one model.

Match the model to the workload. Gemini 3.1 Pro is built for deep, multi-step reasoning, and it brings that same depth to every request, including short lookups that don't need it. For a workload made mostly of quick checks and extractions, a Flash configuration is the better fit, and Pro is best saved for the tasks that need its reasoning depth. Model configurations can also apply different safety settings to security-related prompts. In our run, the Pro configuration declined two short code-security review prompts that Flash answered. If your agent performs security reviews, test those prompts on the configuration you plan to use.

Other ways to build the router. Jev is one way to get a fast classifier, but not the only one. The Getting started with discriminative models codelab runs the same Choice, Score and Noul questions on DiffusionGemma, Google DeepMind's open-weights model, hosted on a Compute Engine GPU VM or on Cloud Run in your own Google Cloud project. An open-source server exposes the same API in front of it, so the routing code in this article only needs a different endpoint. Our results come from Jev, so measure accuracy and latency on your own tasks before switching, and keep in mind that a self-hosted model is billed by the GPU-hour rather than by the token.

Taken together, the results give three practical rules.

Start with Flash on low thinking before you build a router. It solved all 50 tasks and cost considerably less than the default setting. Lowering the output token limit is not a substitute, because it doesn't reduce how much the model thinks on easy tasks. Set the thinking level directly, with thinkingLevel: "LOW".

Use Jev to route short, standalone tasks. Send simple tasks to Flash-Lite and hard ones to Flash on low thinking. Ask Jev one simple yes-or-no question per factor. In our test, this helped reduce cost and response time compared with running Flash on low thinking for everything, and came close to what a perfect router would achieve. Keep long, context-heavy turns on a single model so caching keeps working. For high-volume warehouse workloads, Jeff Nelson's BigQuery and Cloud Run cascade pattern applies the same idea.

Measure what your agent actually spends. Send your agent's traces and thinking-token counts to Cloud Logging and BigQuery, so you can see which tasks drive your spend and catch truncation or retries that inflate it. The benchmark code will be published after open-source review.

In summary, the most cost-effective way to run an agent is to match each task to the model that fits it. Start with a fast model on a light setting. You'll often find it already gets the job done. Then add a small, almost free classifier like Jev to send only the hard tasks to a stronger model, and ask simple yes-or-no questions rather than one broad one. Judge every option by what it costs per task done right, not per token.

#10073. Agent Distraction

What is easy for humans to skim past in code, agents see as a call to action. They do not know better, latching on to that which is littered across the files read during the planning and research phase of the coding journey.

As agents' agency through tools and skills grows the ability for side-quests scales proportionally. Obsolete specs, long resolved bugs, and lagging documentation no longer rest in long forgotten corners of the codebase, but rather are unintentionally ingested as context indirecting and misdirecting the next wave of coders - the agents. This indirection is not free: in the best case it only costs tokens, steps, and time - in the worst case it distracts and grounds the agent on falsehoods leading to incorrect logic and decisions during implementation.

Measuring how often agents fall into these traps across millions of monthly sessions is impossible with manual human review - we need an objective signal derivable from the code itself. Inline TODO(bug/...) comments provide the perfect proxy. TODOs tend to be left behind long after the underlying bug is resolved or abandoned, while the linked bug ticket acts as the canonical record. By cross-referencing every TODO an agent encounters against the TODO's bug status and the user's prompt, we can automatically separate valid work from wasted detours at scale.

By leveraging the distributed traces of agent interactions across thousands of engineers and over hundreds of millions of individual agent steps, we quantify the impact of TODO distractions in the codebase and how agents act on them:

Controlling for developer, codebase complexity, task type, model tier, number of files read, initial prompt length, and the step where the bug reference appeared, using a multi-way fixed-effects regression with developer-clustered standard errors, we see that unprompted bug detours add substantial overhead (all stat sig p<0.0001). Per session:

The Obsolete Detour: In the following trajectory we can observe how this drift plays out. During an investigation into an unrelated bug The agent views SurfaceControlTest.java and sees // TODO(bug/XXX)

This bug, while fixed in 2023, remains lingering in the codebase leading to subsequent investigation distraction across Steps with the agent digging into the bug to learn more.

The Eager Agent: In the trajectory the agent encountered a TODO in the bug it was investigating and decided (unprompted) to "fix" the code

The agent executed multiple Code Search and internal knowledge search queries for the bug ultimately resulting in the agent changing the ModelDownloaderV1 code. Later in the trajectory the human challenged the scope creep.

With the model when admitting it was an incorrect increase in scope:

While in both of these cases they were only trivial to minor detours - they were real distractions costing time, tokens, and human intervention.

As part of addressing this finding at scale we created agents that scrubbed the totality of our codebases, finding bug references in the code that were marked as fixed or obsolete for cleanup. That step alone however was not enough to determine if the TODOs in the codebase were load-bearing or not. The agents had to go further looking at the history of the bug, the file, and changes to the codebase, at times spanning years of history. Only in cases where the agent was able to confirm that the TODO and the intent behind the TODO was obsolete did our agent send a change for review to delete it from the codebase. As a result of this multi-layer approach, our todo cleaner has been able to remove thousands of actually obsolete references over the last 6 months exceeding 95% acceptance from human reviewers.

In recap, as we task agents on more and more ambitious problems, "agent friendly codebases" require more than just the code in the hotpath being healthy. The forgotten corners of the codebase now more than ever carry a significant tax levied against agents.

Tooling like presubmit analyzers, entire corpus scanners, and automated coding agents to remediate dead-todos offer out of the box ready to scale solutions to address the tax enabling a healthier and distraction free codebase for agents to thrive.

Projects that once were on the backburner to cleanup lingering debt but deprioritized due to perceived low value need to be reevaluated with the new agents acting at scale on your codebase.

#10071. NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

New guidance provides a basic framework for less-technical solo business owners, but it may miss the mark on how to secure technology that requires no human oversight.

Threat actors always target the path of least resistance, and for years that has been small to midsize businesses (SMBs). Now, new guidance from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) aims to help companies with possibly even fewer resources: "solopreneurs."

Cybersecurity White Paper 50 (CSWP) is a series of recommendations on how to curb cyber-risks for a population that makes up 81.9% of all US businesses. NIST is trying to offset challenges with guidance for password hygiene, ransomware threats, and adhering to regulations requirements — areas where solopreneurs typically lack the time, money, or people to build out a security program on their own.

The guide translates its Cybersecurity Framework into lay language for non-employer firms, the agency states. But with 33 pages to work through, is it worth the investment?

Most of the practical core is within reach for solopreneurs, says Martin Zugec, technical solutions director at Bitdefender. People just need to scroll to the short list on page 2, which calls for phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (MFA), a password manager, a standard (non-admin) account for daily work, automatic updates, and tested backups with one copy kept offline.

Related:As Test Takers Turn to AI, Exam Security Plays Catch-Up

"None of that needs a security background, and you can do it in an afternoon," Zugec tells Dark Reading.

Compared to other NIST technical publications, Zugec says the CSWP is much easier to digest. Like NIST advertised, the language is plain and every action comes with a reason, a first step, and a note on what changes as businesses grow, he adds.

NIST outlines how businesses can respond to growing contractual agreements and an increasing number of suppliers and third parties as they expand operations and it becomes even more crucial to know third-parties' cyber postures. That means staying current with regulations and establishing a formal process to manage risks that relationships could introduce.

While Bryson Byrd, cybersecurity advisor at Huntress, applauds NIST for the guidance, he says terms like "least privilege," "risk register," and "data sensitivity classification" aren't the language of someone running a bakery or a consulting practice.

"For too long, solopreneurs have been an afterthought in cybersecurity guidance," Byrd tells Dark Reading. "The intent is right, but the closer guidance like this gets to the language of everyday business owners, the more likely it is to actually get implemented."

But it's not just the language, Byrd says. It also assumes the owner knows how to turn on logging, review account sessions, and work though a separate spreadsheet of worksheets. And he points to a recommendation on obtaining legal counsel's input before notifying customers following an incident as an extra cost that often is not in the budget.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

The guidance doesn't appear to take into consideration that "nobody goes into business to build the most secure company that exists," he adds, but to build something over time. Every hour a solopreneur spends on asset inventories, backup testing, tabletop exercises, and compliance tracking is an hour taken away from running the business.

"Asking a single person to do all of this is extraordinarily cumbersome and, quite frankly, unrealistic," Byrd says.

Byrd notes gaps in the guidance in places "we see hurt small businesses in the real world." The first is domain registrar; attackers regularly go after small business domains to launch impersonation attacks and siphon money from customers and partners. Control of the domain means threat actors assume control over email and the business's website.

"Locking down the registrar account with multifactor authentication, enabling registrar lock, and turning on auto-renewal should be part of any baseline for a solopreneur," Byrd recommends.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

The second gap he addresses is email authentication. The three core protocols — Sender Policy Framework, DomainKeys Identified Mail, and Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance — are becoming more important to protect a business from being impersonated and to ensure its legitimate email is delivered, Byrd explains.

The third and perhaps most impactful gap for a business of one is what happens when the owner is unavailable for an extended period of time, whether due to an illness, family matter, or simply a well-deserved vacation.

Ransomware groups target businesses during off-hours, weekends, and holidays. If something does happen that demands an immediate response, it's essential for someone to be there. It could mean the difference between an incident and a breach.

"A break-glass plan that gives a trusted person or partner emergency access to critical accounts is still needed, and it belongs in any cybersecurity plan for a solopreneur," he advises.

Previously, SMBs and the self-employed adopted the mindset that they were too small to be considered a target. That has since been disproven and is only worsening.

Advancements in autonomous tools and artificial intelligence (AI) have lowered the barrier to entry and the cost of attacks, letting threat actors target that population at scale. They realized they had a choice: go after large enterprises with strong defenses for one big payout or target thousands of small shops with weak security that are far more likely to pay up.

As the struggles evolved, so must the guidance. Daniel Eliot, lead for small business engagement at NIST, says the new whitepaper comes nearly a decade after its predecessor, NISTIR 7621 rev.1. After the initial call for comments, "that feedback was instrumental in moving the project forward."

AI is forcing a lot of security guidance to be updated and making that guidance easier to write, says Zugec, adding that new CSWP additions include a section on AI and a warning that AI makes phishing more convincing.

NIST urges businesses to take a second or third look at any message that asks people to click a link, download a file, transfer funds, or log into an account.

But contrary to popular belief, AI hasn't brought any new or novel attacks, Zugec says. It is changing who runs businesses and what they rely on to operate.

Solopreneurs are using AI assistants to read their mailboxes, run commands, write code, and use accounts under the owner's identity, he explains. While it enables one person to do the work of a small team, it also expands the attack surface.

"Many solopreneurs will use agentic AI to grow faster than their security does," he says. "The guide gives no advice on what these agents should be allowed to reach or on securing the code they write."

The biggest gap Zugec says he found in the guide is "AI that acts." NIST treats AI as something passive that businesses need to inventory and review outputs for, but agentic AI has increasingly removed humans from the equation.

As agentic AI enables more people to run a business alone, the security of those businesses matters more than ever, Zugec says. That will warrant outside help, as people increasingly turn to vibe coding to build their own applications. He also urges solopreneurs to have their code reviewed by someone with coding and security experience before anything ships.

If anything is public-facing, an attacker can reach it. That warrants protection.

"AI is good at producing software that works but not necessarily software with a small attack surface," he says. "The guide doesn't cover this, yet it's often the first risk solopreneurs run into."

Zugec points out other weaknesses, too. For example, NIST pushed for continuous updates, but a solopreneur can’t realistically track every legal and contractual security requirement, negotiate security terms with a cloud provider, or monitor their systems around the clock.

Second, it never ranks tasks, which makes prioritization difficult for a one-person team. For example, it opens with governance, the least actionable task, while MFA and backup advice only starts on page 14. It also fails to cover two common attack routes: ClickFix, which tricks people into pasting a command themselves, and a malware that steals their logged-in session, which bypasses MFA

"It lists around 25 actions and says outright that it isn't a checklist, so a busy owner has to decide what comes first," Zugec says.

The guide also sets its scope by head count, which is problematic. Technically the head count would be one, but risk follows what information businesses hold and who targets them. But it's not just about size; it's about what's exposed. Risk heavily varies between someone who sells candles on Etsy as a side gig versus someone in the finance industry trading billions in cryptocurrency.

"A solo crypto operator or a consultant with client secrets needs far more than the guide’s baseline," Zugec says.

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#10065. What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Today, we announce the General Availability of Pathways on Google Cloud Platform. In this post, you will learn about Pathways, the distributed system Google built to train its own large models, including Gemini. We discuss how Pathways addresses the coordination challenge by introducing one client that describes the whole computation as a graph, and how the distributed runtime places it, moves the tensors, and keeps the accelerators busy.

Most large-model training runs as Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) programs. Every accelerator runs the same program in lockstep and coordinates through collectives like AllReduce.

It works well when your job is the same program running on every device. It struggles when the job is no longer uniform, like a pipeline whose stages wait on each other or an RL loop where a sampler, a reward model, and a trainer are different programs that have to overlap.

Large runs also have to survive hardware failures, which interrupted Gemini 2.5 training multiple times per hour. In SPMD, one lost machine stops every process and sends the run back to its last checkpoint. In each case, the challenge is coordination. You have to decide what runs where and in what order, how tensors move between devices, and how the job keeps going when a machine drops out.

In this post of the series “Pathways on Google Cloud”, you will learn about Pathways, the distributed system Google built to train its own large models, including Gemini. The post discusses how Pathways addresses the coordination challenge by introducing one client that describes the whole computation as a graph, and how the distributed runtime places it, moves the tensors, and keeps the accelerators busy.

By the end, you'll know where SPMD is suboptimal, what single-controller execution changes, and how Pathways coordinates a whole training job across a cluster.

If you train PyTorch models, you almost certainly use Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) or Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP). DDP runs a copy of your script on every accelerator and averages gradients with a collective operation such as AllReduce. FSDP shards parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across workers so that the model fits at all.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

DDP and FSDP both follow the Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) execution model. Every process runs the same copy of your script, owns its accelerators for the whole run, and moves in lockstep with the others, because the only way they coordinate is through collectives like AllReduce. Inside one tightly connected group of accelerators those collectives run over a fast interconnect and are cheap. Scale the job across groups and the same collectives cross the datacenter network, which is far slower. On a TPU v5p, for example, each chip gets 1,200 GB/s of bidirectional chip-to-chip bandwidth inside its group, but only 50 Gb/s (gigabits, about 6 GB/s) to the datacenter network which is roughly two orders of magnitude less.

And because every step blocks on its collectives, that communication lands directly in step time. The more groups you span, the larger the share of each step spent moving data, so throughput grows slower than the number of accelerators you add.

As long as your training job is one program that fills the hardware you give it, this execution model fits well. You write your model as if there were one device, and the collectives do the rest. But fitting a model into memory is only part of the problem. Keeping every accelerator busy is the harder part, and this is where the SPMD model starts to show its limits.

Take pipeline parallelism as an example. You split a model into blocks across devices, and each device now runs different code over smaller micro-batches. Activations flow forward, activation gradients flow back, and while device 0 works on the first micro-batch, devices 1 and 2 wait. Apart from the idle accelerators you keep paying for, this drops utilization and throughput, even though every device has work in the steady state.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Another example is RL post-training for an LLM. You have a sampler that generates rollouts, a reward model that scores them, and a trainer that updates the policy and sends the new weights back to the sampler. These are three different programs that should overlap; otherwise the sampler is idle while the trainer runs, and the trainer is idle while the sampler generates.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

In both scenarios, the job is now several different programs running on different devices, and their dependencies can no longer be managed through a single collective. You now have to coordinate which devices share which tensors, which processes run while others are still finishing, and how early to enqueue the next buffer so an accelerator never waits for input. Because each worker only has visibility into its local devices and data, no individual process can manage all of these dependencies itself. That has several consequences.

First, because each process owns its accelerators for the whole run and every collective blocks until all devices finish, one failed machine prevents the collective from completing and stops the entire job, forcing a restart from the last checkpoint. You cannot add devices mid-run, and you cannot give devices back.

Second, because each process holds its accelerators from start to finish, capacity can't move to where it's needed. Within one job, a stage that needs fewer chips than another still keeps the extra ones. They sit idle, you keep paying for them, and no other part of the job can use them until the run ends. Across a team, the same happens at cluster scale. Every job owns its accelerators for as long as it runs, so sharing a cluster means splitting it into per-job allocations, and each new job brings up its own processes on its own hosts.

Finally, the development process itself gets harder. On one host you iterate fast because you run the script, drop into a Python shell, set a breakpoint, and debug. This is not true once the job spans many hosts. You need a launcher to push your script to every host, you hit coordination bugs that never showed up on one machine, and there's no single process to break into. When something hangs, each worker is stuck at a collective waiting for the others, with no one place that shows the whole job.

So the common challenge here is the coordination itself. As soon as the job stops being one program in lockstep, you have to decide what runs where, in what order, and how tensors get from one device to the next.

One way to describe this is as a graph, where each block is a node, each tensor that moves between blocks is an edge, and the devices are where the nodes are placed. You can wire that graph up by hand in SPMD, one process at a time. But what if a single client declared that graph, including what each block does, what it needs, and where it runs, and a distributed runtime handled the transfers, dependencies, and ordering along its edges?

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

That is the idea behind Pathways, the distributed system Google built to train its own largest models, including Gemini. Pathways runs JAX programs on TPUs and it is available on Google Cloud.

With Pathways, you define the end-to-end computation from a single Python client, without writing custom coordination code, and a distributed runtime executes it. That client is decoupled from the hardware. It runs on an ordinary CPU machine and you write your program against virtual devices; a resource manager maps them onto real chips, and a worker on each accelerator host runs the compiled programs it receives.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Because your code refers to virtual devices rather than physical ones, the runtime is flexible to allow users to change the devices used for a given computation. This allows you to stay in control while the runtime handles the mapping to hardware. In an RL loop, for example, the trainer and the samplers rarely want the same number of chips, so you can give the sampler stage more chips by asking for more virtual devices.

Also, the same capability helps when a host fails or the hardware isn't ready yet. If a host dies, the resource manager remaps the work onto healthy chips and the run keeps going instead of relaunching the whole job, which is the basis for elastic training. And because the program targets virtual devices, compilation can start before the physical chips are provisioned, so setup overlaps with provisioning instead of waiting on it.

The resource manager owning the chips also means one Pathways cluster can serve several clients, so researchers on a team can share its capacity. With the Shared Pathways Service, the cluster stays up as a long running service, which lets you develop interactively on TPUs hosted on GKE. Each client connects on demand from a laptop or VM, gets its own slices (groups of tightly connected TPU chips) from the shared pool, and hands them back when it disconnects. When every chip is busy, the next workload waits until capacity frees up.

Take the three-block model from Figure 2. Block A runs on one group of devices, block B on a second, block C on a third. You declare what each block computes, its target devices, and where its outputs go. Pathways expresses those dependencies as a distributed dataflow graph, in which each block is a compiled SPMD program and each edge is a tensor the runtime has to deliver.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

In a single SPMD program, the framework handles the collectives that keep the devices in sync within a group, with or without Pathways, and your code doesn't change. The difference shows up once the job runs several programs on different groups (Multiple Programs, Multiple Data, MPMD), like these three blocks or the sampler, reward model, and trainer of an RL loop. Then no single process sees both sides (the same limit from before, where each worker only knows its own devices), so getting a tensor from block A to block B is a hand-off you have to coordinate yourself.

Pathways closes that gap. You declare the dependency once, and the runtime moves and reshards the tensor for you, over the fast interconnect within a group and over the datacenter network between groups.

To keep the accelerators busy, Pathways prepares launches ahead of time with futures and parallel asynchronous dispatch. While block A is still computing, block B can't run yet, but its input shapes and dtypes are already known, so the runtime allocates B's buffers and schedules the transfer before A's output even exists. Host-side setup for every block happens up front, and each block launches when its inputs arrive.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

This is also what keeps the single client from becoming a bottleneck. Because dispatch is asynchronous, the coordination work overlaps with the compute already running on the chips, so the client stays off the critical path instead of stalling the accelerators between steps.

In Pathways, the runtime decides execution order when a group has more than one operation ready. In pipelined training, B's devices often hold both the forward pass for an upcoming micro-batch and the backward pass for an earlier one. If each device picked on its own, their collectives would conflict and the group would stall.

Pathways has a central scheduler that puts every program's operations into one consistent order, so operations that must communicate start together instead of deadlocking.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

And because it's still one client, the development loop we mentioned before comes back. It's the same single Python process whether you drive one host or thousands of hosts, so you can drop into a shell, set a breakpoint, and inspect the run as it goes. When something stalls, there's one place that knows what's queued on every device and which dependency hasn't been met, instead of a hang spread across separate processes.

Put together, Pathways separates model building from execution. You choose how the model partitions across hardware using the client. And the runtime handles the transfers, ordering, and scheduling that keep accelerators busy, across the whole cluster rather than just your slice of it.

Described this way, Pathways can start to sound like an orchestrator you already know. If scheduling work, moving tensors, and keeping a whole cluster busy brings Ray to mind, it should. But the two work at different layers.

Ray is an open-source framework for orchestrating Python-native AI workloads across large clusters. It provisions the cluster, schedules your Python code as tasks and actors, and launches your workload across hosts, holding data loading, training, serving, and tuning under one control plane. To Ray, an accelerator is a resource to schedule.

What Ray doesn't change is how your training runs on the chips. The job inside each worker still runs as SPMD. The framework inserts the collectives, and each process sees only its own devices. Ray places and starts that job but it doesn't turn it into a single program that drives the whole cluster.

That is the layer Pathways works at. It changes the execution model underneath, so one client coordinates every chip. Because they sit at different layers, the two are complementary. In principle, Ray can orchestrate the cluster and the pipeline while Pathways handles how the training step executes.

So concretely, Ray's job is about orchestration while Pathways' job is about execution. With Ray, you tie your data, training, serving, and tuning together and spread heterogeneous work across accelerators and clouds. With Pathways, you run one model across many groups of chips, express patterns beyond SPMD, and recover from a failed host instead of relaunching the whole job.

When a training job stops being one uniform program, the challenge becomes coordinating the dependencies between stages, the tensors that cross the network, and the ordering that keeps every accelerator fed.

SPMD requires you to address these dependencies. With Pathways, you describe the computation once, from a single client, as a graph of blocks and the tensors between them. And you have a runtime that places the blocks on virtual devices, moves and reshards the tensors, orders the work across the cluster, and remaps around a failed host.

With Pathways, model building and execution are separated and you reason about the whole cluster instead of one slice of it.

#10060. Security Update on PHP2Shell: Impact for Docker Customers

Secure, minimal container images for every team, free with enterprise features, if needed.

On Tuesday, October 20, 2026, Docker began tracking two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, commonly known as PHP2Shell. The vulnerabilities allow attackers to execute code remotely in PHP core, and they affect PHP packages going back to version 5.4: the supported versions 8.2 through 8.5, and the end-of-life versions 5.x, 7.x, 8.0, and 8.1.

To address these vulnerabilities, PHP released 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, and advised anyone running PHP to update to the latest version immediately.

Although this is a vulnerability in PHP itself, not in Docker’s systems, it nonetheless affects Docker users who build on PHP images and packages. In response, we have updated the Docker Hardened Images and Docker Official Images on Docker Hub, and advise customers to immediately update.

Along with other package repositories and secure package providers, Docker has been made aware of and is tracking two recently discovered critical vulnerabilities in PHP packages distributed since version 5.4. The two critical vulnerabilities, now commonly referred to as “PHP2Shell,” are identified and tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. (The PHP Foundation has published a detailed report on the discovery that we recommend reading for full context.)

In short: these vulnerabilities could allow remote code execution in PHP core by malicious actors. Both are flaws in how PHP manages request memory. In CVE-2026-109618, when PHP runs out of memory mid-request and aborts, some code paths leave memory uninitialized, and PHP’s cleanup step then reads it. In CVE-2026-109619, PHP’s internal state can keep pointing at memory that has already been freed, and a later request then uses that stale state. Attackers have multiple ways to trigger either condition and turn it into remote code execution.

Affected versions include the currently supported versions (8.2 through 8.5), as well as the EOL and unsupported versions 5.x, 7.x, 8.0, and 8.1.

Whether you are a Docker user or not, if you are using any of the above affected versions of PHP, you should immediately upgrade to the latest version. That includes PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, or 8.5.12, or a later release in the corresponding branch.

There is no other comprehensive remediation for the affected versions. Updating is the only complete mitigation path.

If for any reason you are unable to complete an immediate update, we strongly recommend taking your system offline until such time that you can initiate mitigation. This the guidance of not only Docker, but of the FBI, and numerous experts throughout the cybersecurity community.

While this vulnerability exists in PHP itself and not directly in Docker’s systems, there is nonetheless potential risk and exposure to Docker customers who run PHP in their applications, including anyone using PHP images or packages from Docker Hub, Docker Official Images, or Docker Hardened Images.

For users of Docker Official Images:Docker Official Images have already been updated and released to Docker Hub and mirrored to Amazon ECR. Customers using either of these sources should update immediately.

For users of Docker Hardened Images (DHI):Docker Hardened Images have already been updated and released to Docker Hub. The currently supported versions of PHP were updated as follows:

The updates to our images were completed and released within 24-hours of the upstream patches being made available. These images were made available after successfully executing the DHI testing and verification processes.

If you have any issues accessing the updated images or migrating to the new versions, please contact Docker Support at app.docker.com/support/contact. As always when it comes to matters of security, we appreciate your diligence.

Two security events landed side by side this week, PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise. Both reached the same place, the foundation their applications are built on.

PHP2Shell is a pair of critical flaws in the PHP engine itself, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. They let an unauthenticated request become code execution on the server, on any PHP application, however careful its own code is, and PHP runs about 69% of the websites whose server-side language is known.

The eMudhra compromise is a different kind of problem. Eight intermediate certificates from the certificate authority eMudhra turned out to have private keys that can be computed from the public certificates, which let anyone issue a certificate for any website and have it accepted. Browsers revoke certificates like these on their own, but a container image carries its own trust store and keeps trusting them until it is rebuilt.

The dhi.io/php image was rebuilt on the patched PHP and published early on October 22, within 24 hours of the upstream release and after the DHI testing and verification steps. Pulling the current tag puts you on the fixed version. The few DHI images that bundle their own PHP application, such as composer and nextcloud, follow as their upstream projects release.

The certificate compromise touched the whole catalog, because every image carries a trust store. In the 48 hours after the PHP release, the DHI build system ran 16,567 package and image builds across the catalog. By 10pm UTC on October 22, almost all catalog tags were on the fixed CA store, with most of the rest in the build queue. That percentage comes from the SBOM that ships with every image, read for every published tag to check which CA store and which PHP version it carries, and you can run the same check on anything you pull.

If you run PHP on Docker Hardened Images, pull the current tag for your branch and redeploy, and rebuild anything you built on top of a DHI image so it picks up the new base docker pull dhi.io/php:8.4

Customizations built through the DHI Enterprise workflow are rebuilt automatically when the base layer is patched. For the certificate fix the same applies to every image you build from a DHI base, PHP or not. The Docker Security update from October 22 lists the affected PHP versions and the support path.

If you run PHP in any other container, check the PHP version running inside it rather than the tag on the outside, and rebuild it on a patched base.

Weeks like this one will keep coming, but a trusted foundation will make all the difference.

If you are not building on hardened images yet, this week is the wake-up call and the week to start. Both events landed on the foundation, and that is where the fix has to happen, in the image itself, rebuilt from fixed sources before anyone pulls it.

This is exactly what Docker Hardened Images were built for. Docker builds, patches and maintains the system packages inside each image from source, and the build system is event-driven, so an upstream release or a changed package triggers rebuilds of everything that depends on it. Each image ships signed, with its SBOM, SLSA Build Level 3 provenance and VEX data attached, which is why a rebuild of this size can be measured as well as done.

The catalog is free and open source under Apache 2.0, with near-zero CVEs on every image. It stays compatible with the Alpine and Debian your teams already run, so adoption is a one-line change to the FROM line in your Dockerfile, with no migration project attached. DHI Select and DHI Enterprise add SLA-backed remediation with critical CVE fixes within 7 days, FIPS and STIG variants, image customization with the guarantees kept, and Extended Lifecycle Support for the versions upstream has stopped patching. All of it is in the Docker Hardened Images catalog, free to pull today.

Principal Product Marketing Manager, Docker

Vishrut Iyengar is Principal PMM for Security at Docker, focused on Docker Hardened Images, supply chain security, and securing what AI agents build.

#10056. Win the Agentic Era, Together: Introducing the Docker Navigator Partner Program

Secure, minimal container images for every team, free with enterprise features, if needed.

Over the past year, almost every conversation I’ve had with a partner has ended in the same place. Their customers are moving AI agents out of the lab and into production, and the moment they do, the question changes. It stops being “Can we build this?” and becomes “Can we trust it, secure it, and govern it?” The partners who can answer that second set of questions are the partners customers keep.

Today, we are launching the Docker Navigator Partner Program to help you become that partner. This post explains what we’ve built, why we built it around AI governance, and how you can get the most from it.

AI adoption is not following a normal technology curve. Every team, every vendor, every model provider, and every hyperscaler is racing to ship agentic capability, and no single company sees the whole stack. Identity, observability, supply chain security, MCP gateways, models, and clouds are each building their piece. What enterprises are missing is a trusted, common layer that lets those pieces work together safely.

That’s Docker’s role. Docker is where agents, models, and tools actually run: vertically integrated where it matters, and horizontally open to everything our customers already use. We describe it as being the Trusted Navigator for the agentic era; the constant that helps customers make sense of a landscape moving faster than any one team can track.

Partners are how that promise reaches customers. Whether you build technology, run a cloud, deliver services, or sell through the channel, you extend our reach and turn the Docker platform into a complete, governable stack. So the program carries the same name, and its tiers describe the journey a partner takes with us.

Every partner in the Docker Navigator Partner Program is navigating the agentic era with Docker. The tiers mark how far along that journey you are, and the top tier carries the program’s name on purpose: it’s the title you earn when you have shown you can navigate it for customers.

If you’re already a Docker partner, you enter the new program at the tier that matches your status today. Nothing is taken away, and your tier is protected until 30 April 2027 while we work with you on the requirements.

We designed the benefits around one principle: the more you invest in building a governed AI practice on Docker, the more Docker invests in you. At the top tier, that means:

The commercial model rewards what you bring:

If you’re working on an AI governance opportunity today, register it. Everything lives in one place: the new Docker Navigator Partner Portal, where you register deals, take the free Docker Partner Sales Certification, request MDF, download assets, and track your progress against your tier in real time.

No one wins the agentic era alone, and Docker has spent much of 2026 demonstrating our belief in a collaborative ecosystem and approach. For example, in September, Docker became a founding member of the Blueprint Alliance alongside Okta, AWS, CrowdStrike, Databricks, Google Cloud, Lovable, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Wiz and Zscaler, with GE Appliances and World Central Kitchen serving as strategic advisors. Announced at Oktane in Las Vegas, the Alliance has agreed on a shared architecture for securing AI agents, built around four questions every enterprise is asking: Where are my agents? What can they do? What are they doing? How do I respond? Our part is the environment where agents execute: isolation, runtime governance, and a secure supply chain that extends trust beyond the model to the place the agent runs.

Mat Velloso, our Chief Product Officer, and I recorded a 20-minute conversation for partners on why Docker sits where the agentic era is being decided, where the AI governance opportunity is opening up, and what it means for your business. It’s the fastest way to get your sales and technical teams on the same page. After you log in to the Docker Navigator Partner Portal, you can watch the recording here.

Not yet a partner? Start at https://www.docker.com/partners/register/.

This is a new program for Docker, and we’re humble enough to know we won’t have everything perfect on day one. We want your feedback and input. Tell us what’s missing. We’ll listen, we’ll be open with you, and we’ll invest in your success.
