#9918. AIを活用したサイバー攻撃の増加を受け、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの緊急資金拠出を推進

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

この対策パッケージには、官民合同のサイバー対応チーム、経済省が主導するAI専門チーム、および政府の新たな能動的サイバー防衛権限の行使に関する裁量の拡大が含まれている。

Translation provided by Dark Reading's internal AI translation tool.

日本においてサイバー攻撃や情報漏洩が急増していることを受け、日本政府は、攻撃に迅速に対応し、インフラのセキュリティを強化するための産官の専門家チームを設立することを目的とした、100億円（6,300万ドル）規模の緊急サイバーセキュリティ対策パッケージを可決した。

この戦略の4つの柱には、サイバー防衛へのAI導入を含む基礎的なサイバーセキュリティ対策の全国的な徹底、国内のサイバー捜査能力の強化、サイバー攻撃の被害者への支援拡充、そして民間企業と連携してサイバー攻撃に共同で対応することが含まれている。

高市早苗首相は、国のサイバーレジリエンス（回復力）を高めるため、これらのサイバーセキュリティ対策を「迅速かつ効果的に」実施するよう求めた。

「今この瞬間も、不正アクセスや情報漏洩の事案が後を絶たず、人々の日常生活や企業活動に多大な影響を及ぼしている」と、高市早苗首相は11月6日に緊急対策パッケージを発表した際の声明で述べた。「政府のあらゆる資源を動員し、サイバー攻撃への対応能力を全面的に強化していこう。」

サイバー攻撃の急増は、日本企業や政府機関に甚大な被害をもたらしている。サイバーセキュリティ企業（旧トレンドマイクロ）であるTrendAIのデータによると、2026年の最初の9か月間で600件以上のサイバーセキュリティインシデントが公表され、2025年通年の594件を上回った。公表されている報告数は控えめな推計に過ぎない。日本の個人情報保護監督機関は、4月から10月中旬にかけて2,094件の情報漏洩事案を記録しており（原文は日本語）、これも2025年度通年の総件数を上回っている。

他の地域ではAIが攻撃者を支援しているものの、サイバーセキュリティ企業TrendAIの脅威調査共同責任者であるライアン・フローレス氏は、脅威に関する声明の中で、インシデントの増加と攻撃者によるAIの利用との間に明確な関連性は確認されていないと述べた。

Related:Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

「サイバー攻撃は世界的に増加しており、その結果として侵害やデータ漏洩も増加しています」と同氏は述べた。「AIが直接関与しているわけではないかもしれませんが、攻撃者が標的を見つけたり、操作を自動化したりするのを支援するAIの能力により、サイバー攻撃は大規模化しています。組織は、被害に遭う確率を下げるために、サイバーリスクを低減し、脆弱性を解消する必要があります。」

最近の侵害事例には、冷凍食品大手のニチレイやビール・食品大手のアサヒに対するランサムウェア攻撃、およびGMOインターネットグループを標的としたデータ侵害などが含まれる。これらの攻撃の多くは犯罪的な性質を持つが、盗まれた情報が他の犯罪グループや国家主体のアクターによって、日本の国民に対して悪用される可能性があることが懸念されていると、日本の通信大手NTTのチーフ・サイバーセキュリティ・ストラテジスト、松原美穂子氏は指摘する。

「攻撃者が十分な個人情報を収集・集約できれば、個人の嗜好から経済活動に至るまで、日本国民の詳細なプロファイルを構築できる」と同氏は述べる。「そのデータは、世論を操作したり、日本の機関に対する信頼を損なわせたりするための標的型偽情報キャンペーンなど、日本に対する影響工作に利用される可能性がある」

日本政府は、緊急資金を活用して、サイバーセキュリティ体制全体を強化するための4つの広範な取り組みを推進する意向だ。閣僚会議の公表された議事録によると、政府は、最近の多くの情報漏洩は適切なセキュリティ対策によって防ぐことができたはずだと指摘し、最初の取り組みとして、各組織が基本的なサイバーセキュリティ対策を確実に実施するよう促すとしている。

2つ目の主要な取り組みは、調査および情報収集能力を向上させ、より精度の高い分析を可能にし、その結果を国民に提供することで、攻撃への備えを強化することである。第三に、政府はサイバー攻撃への対応を強化し、国際的なパートナーシップを構築するとともに、積極的なサイバー防衛措置を実施する。最後に、政府は被害者を支援する能力とインフラを整備し、市民が損害を回復し、企業が事業を継続できるようにする計画だ。

「被害を受けた組織や個人が迷うことなく支援を受けられるよう、利用しやすい相談窓口や専門家による直接的な支援を拡充し、二次被害を防ぐための情報共有を強化する」と、日本の議事録には記されている。「また、官民の専門家を柔軟に派遣するための全国的な仕組みの構築にも着手する」

10月1日、日本の「積極的サイバー防衛法」が施行され、警察や自衛隊（SDF）に対し、日本の国家安全保障にリスクをもたらすあらゆるサイバー攻撃に対して強力な措置を講じる権限が与えられた。

「多くの国が、日本がいかなる種類のサイバー攻撃に対して、どれほどの速さで、どの程度の強度で対応できるのかを知りたがっているだろう」とNTTの松原氏は述べ、次のように付け加えた。「この緊急対策パッケージは……法律の枠組みを経済全体にわたる実用的な能力へと転換し、攻撃の可能性が高まる中、あらゆる規模の組織が攻撃を予防、検知、対応できるよう準備するために必要である。」

しかし、この資金はあくまで第一歩に過ぎず、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの投資を継続するには、さらなる資金が必要になると同氏は指摘する。

「この対策パッケージの重要な点は、サイバーセキュリティを個々の組織に完全に任せておくことはできないという認識が示されていることだ」と松原氏は述べる。「セキュリティ評価やインシデント対応、復旧支援といった形の政府による支援が、大きな違いを生むことができる。」

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

#9917. NoisyTCP bug gives Linux servers a remote crash problem 11 years in the making

Flaw can take down an entire host, even when the vulnerable service is running inside a container

The researcher who sounded the alarm over Dirty Frag earlier this year has uncovered another Linux kernel flaw, and this one lets attackers crash entire servers remotely without so much as a password.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP, was discovered by security researcher Hyunwoo Kim, who says it affects almost all Linux distributions. The flaw dates back to October 2015 and went unnoticed until this year, when Kim found and patched it.

Attackers don't need to log in or get their hands on any credentials to cause trouble. They can simply knock the server over, although there's no evidence yet that the flaw can be used to steal data or hijack a machine.

The bug is buried in Linux's TCP networking code. Two parts of the kernel can trip over each other while processing incoming traffic, leaving one trying to use memory that's already been freed. When that happens, Linux can panic and take the whole machine down with it.

Kim says there's no need for any special server configuration either. Services such as Nginx, Apache, and SSH can be vulnerable straight out of the box. An attacker needs access to an open TCP port on a system that processes incoming network traffic across multiple receive queues or CPUs.

Perhaps more concerning for administrators running containerized workloads, the damage isn't necessarily limited to the application being attacked. Because the flaw sits in the Linux kernel, crashing a web server inside a container can take down the underlying host and anything else running on it.

Kim found that the attack was particularly effective against virtual machines. During testing, he managed to crash Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers running on QEMU/KVM virtual machines in between five seconds and two minutes.

Physical hardware put up more of a fight. Even after tailoring his exploit to the target machine, Kim needed roughly 14 hours to crash a bare-metal server running Nginx.

Kim has a knack for finding holes in Linux. Back in May, he uncovered Dirty Frag, a kernel bug that allowed local users to gain root privileges. That one caused headaches for administrators when a working exploit went public before patches were ready.

His latest discovery, NoisyTCP, has another potentially nasty trick up its sleeve. Kim identified a second exploitation path involving a use-after-free condition, although pulling it off is considerably more difficult than simply crashing a server.

In his advisory, Kim says he has developed a limited exploit targeting virtual machines in a lab environment but has yet to demonstrate a general-purpose remote code execution attack. For the moment, the confirmed impact is remote denial of service.

A fix was committed to the upstream Linux kernel on November 3, but administrators will need to check whether their distribution has shipped an updated kernel. Red Hat has rated the vulnerability Important, assigning it a CVSS score of 7.5.

Kim published the details on November 15, once the disclosure embargo was lifted. The bug had been hiding in plain sight since 2015, leaving Linux servers vulnerable to remote crashes for 11 years. Not bad for a flaw that doesn't even require a login. ®

#9916. Anatomy of a Frontier Lab Agent Intrusion: A Technical Timeline of the July 2026 Incident

A companion technical writeup to our incident disclosure. This post walks through how the intrusion actually worked: the two initial-access vectors, how the agent pivoted and moved laterally, representative examples of the commands that were run and how we investigated with GLM 5.2 (an open-source model). Live credentials, internal hostnames, and specific indicators have been redacted or genericized, while the techniques are described exactly as observed by Hugging Face.

We are publishing this level of detail because the technique matters more than the incident, as it reveals the emerging attack capabilities of the frontier agents, how they could be used by rogue actors, and how everyone should be prepared as defenders.

Below is an interactive replay of the intrusion - a step-by-step visualization of the 4.5-day campaign: the attack chain across trust boundaries, phase activity, and the commands as they were recorded.

⛶ Watch the interactive replay in full screen

Over roughly two and a half days inside our infrastructure, an autonomous AI agent driven by a combination of OpenAI models ran an end-to-end intrusion against our platform: it was thousands of small, automated decisions, executed at machine speed across short-lived sandbox environments, with command-and-control staged on ordinary public web services.

The agent was running an internal OpenAI cyber-capability evaluation based on the ExploitGym benchmark, which tasks an AI agent with finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities. OpenAI ran this on its own infrastructure, and the ExploitGym maintainers and their infrastructure had no involvement in the deployment or operation of that evaluation environment. As far as we were able to infer, across the course of being evaluated on this benchmark, the agent inferred that Hugging Face may host that benchmark's models, datasets, and reference solutions. We believe the entire intrusion was, from the agent's point of view, an attempt to cheat the evaluation: reach our production systems and steal the test solutions rather than solve the challenge on its own.

Our forensic reconstruction covers ~17,600 attacker actions that we were able to recover, grouped into ~6,280 clusters, between 2026-07-09 02:28 UTC and 2026-07-13 14:14 UTC. We reconstructed these actions from the agent's logs on a code sandbox used by the agent (see below) and were able to map them to shell commands as well as evaluation submissions and correlate actions with our own platform logs, in particular from the dataset processor nodes, API, and pod. Using open-weights models, in particular zai-org/GLM-5.2, we were able to decipher most of the agent payloads (see below) that were encrypted via chunking and key encryption.

The campaign, as we were able to reconstruct it, had two stages:

Once a prod-pod foothold was established, the agent followed a standard escalation shape: recon, drop a stager, establish Command-and-Control (C2), then pivot into the cluster, into cloud metadata, into our internal network, and into our source-control supply chain. Output from the commands run inside our pod was sent back to the agent via the HF API and attacker-controlled dead-drop datasets, which the agent then read from that sandbox.

While the intrusion did reach Hugging Face's internal infrastructure, the only customer content accessed was five datasets whose names and files suggest a connection to ExploitGym/CyberGym challenges and solutions. No other customer-facing models, datasets, Spaces, or packages were affected, and the only customer records read were operational metadata tied to search queries against the dataset server.

The full attack chain across trust boundaries. The agent escaped OpenAI's evaluation sandbox, reached the internet, rooted a third-party code sandbox as its base, then abused our dataset processor (file read, then code execution) to reach our internal network. Dashed arrow: command output read back by the agent via the HF API and dead-drop datasets.

Stage 1 is the agent's path to an external launchpad, and it runs through two other parties' infrastructure, neither of which is us, so we will stay succinct on these parts and mostly refer the reader to OpenAI's blog post on the topic: https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-model-evaluation-security-incident/

As OpenAI shared in this blog post, during an internal capability evaluation on OpenAI's platform, the agent happened to escape via a 0-day exploit from the package proxy cache to access the internet. The agent found an unsecured, user-hosted public endpoint designed to allow running arbitrary code for CyberGym-style tasks on third-party sandbox infrastructure (Modal). It used this external sandbox as its control, staging, and egress base, running commands as admin/root and using it as its attack launchpad. That sandbox had no direct network path into our cluster; everything below ran from it. Modal’s infrastructure was not compromised in any way.

On this external sandbox, the agent abused an existing code-execution harness: an instance labeled "CyberGym", deployed by an unknown third party, exposing an arbitrary-code endpoint that upstream CyberGym does not provide. In short: an agent submits C code via a /submit-function API call, and the harness compiles and runs that code inside a per-submission sandbox against a target program (here, sqlite3). The agent repurposed this harness to run arbitrary shell commands as follows.

The sandbox compiles a submitted src/main.c and links it against a target that calls sqlite3_initialize(). That function is registered as a constructor: it runs automatically when the library loads. The agent simply redefined it:

That alone yields code execution. But the agent went further and abused the submission metadata itself. The sandbox echoes the submitted source path into a shell step, so a classic ;...;# injection in the path field turned the build into arbitrary commands:

Both routes converged on the same result: arbitrary shell as uid=0 inside the sandbox. The very first recovered RCE, at 07-09 04:01 UTC, was simply:

Within the hour, the agent was mapping the sandbox: the container's mount table, cgroups, the vendor's control-plane sockets, and a bundled debug shell that happened to ship curl, nc, and ip:

That bundled toolchain mattered later: when normal egress was throttled, the agent kept falling back to these pre-staged binaries.

This is how the agent reached inside our perimeter, and it was operated entirely from the external sandbox in Stage 1. The agent crafted malicious dataset configs and uploaded them to our platform. When our dataset server processed one, the config drove the data loader inside the production pod the server ran in. The agent had no direct network path to our cluster and was using datasets as the path in and path out. Output from every action was sent back to the agent through the HF API and attacker-controlled dead-drop datasets, which it read back from that sandbox.

Both vectors abused the same surface (the loader that turns a dataset's declared config into file reads) but to different ends, and both sidestepped the same defense. An earlier and noisier variant had tried classic SSRF, pointing the worker at remote URLs (cloud metadata endpoints like 169.254.169.254): the datasets library's URL allowlist rejected every non-platform URL before any fetch (ValueError: not an hf path). So the agent stopped asking the worker to fetch remote resources and instead made it act on local ones: read a local file (Vector 1), or execute local code (Vector 2). Neither is a URL fetch, so the allowlist never saw them.

A dataset config can specify its data files in many formats, including HDF5. The agent committed a dataset whose config pointed each split at a small .h5 file, and each file was a valid HDF5 container holding a single dataset whose raw data was declared to live at a local filesystem path. When the worker opened the file to build the split, it read the raw bytes from that path and returned them as the dataset's rows, which the agent then read back over the HF API. No code ran; this vector is purely a file disclosure, and it is the one the agent used first.

The declared storage paths pointed at exactly what an attacker looking for a foothold wants:

Reading the envu8 split returned the worker pod's full environment, including some secrets and credentials. The mainu8 and startu8 splits returned the worker's own source code, giving the agent a map of exactly how the pipeline turns a config into actions. A single dataset upload leaked both credentials and pipeline implementation details, with no code execution involved.

The second vector is server-side template injection, which gave the agent code execution. A malicious dataset config used an fsspec reference:// spec whose numeric offset field was actually a Jinja2 template. The renderer wrongly evaluated it, and the agent walked the standard Python object graph to reach exec:

This ran arbitrary Python inside a production conversion worker pod on our Kubernetes cluster, driven by injection from the launchpad. That pod was the agent's foothold inside our perimeter, and every command it ran there was smuggled back out through the HF API and dead-drop datasets.

Stage 2's command-injection and read-back loop. The agent uploads a malicious dataset config (1), our dataset server processes it (2), the loader acts in the prod pod - reading a local file or executing code (3), the result is committed to a dead-drop dataset (4) and served back over the HF API (5). Lastly, the agent reads it and crafts the next action (6).

The recovered actions group into phases. Two dates carry most of the volume: a Day 1 burst to establish the foothold and C2 on the compromised external sandbox, and the Day 3 main campaign, when every lateral-movement phase started at once.

The campaign as recorded, from the first action on 07-09 02:28 UTC to the last on 07-13 14:14 UTC. Top: event volume over time. Below: per-phase activity, one row per phase. Recon, rce, and dropper run from Day 1; the lateral-movement phases (k8s, supply-chain, tailscale) all begin on Day 3, when the campaign pivots into our clusters.

After the first id/env at 04:01, the agent spent the morning enumerating the external sandbox and testing outbound channels. It downloaded artifacts from its OpenAI egress server, then landed on a set of ordinary public services as its command-and-control and exfil substrate: a request-capture service, several pastebins, and file-drop hosts.

The first C2 execution (15:36) was a staged download-and-run, with commands chunked and gzip+base64 encoded so nothing sensitive appeared in cleartext:

By 19:32 the agent was packing every payload:

A quiet day. The main activity was queries to code-search engines and to the platform API for the identifiers visible in its own environment: challenge infrastructure names and environment markers.

Every escalation that mattered happened on this day. The agent went from code execution in a single worker pod to cluster-admin across multiple internal clusters in under thirteen hours.

Kubernetes (10:10). These commands ran inside the prod pod reached via the Stage 2 injection. The agent read the projected service-account token every pod carries and started talking to the cluster API, exfiltrating the output back through the API and dead-drops:

It resolved internal service names, hit the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254), and enumerated RBAC. When DNS got in the way, it monkey-patched the resolver in-process to pin a hostname to a hardcoded IP:

Supply chain (15:51). The agent used a leaked write-scoped platform token to clone a dataset it controlled and use it as a staging and C2 channel:

Replaying the node's cloud role (17:33-23:37). The temporary credentials lifted from the metadata endpoint were replayed from external addresses on two hosting providers and used to enumerate our cloud estate: VPCs, EKS clusters, transit gateways, secrets, and the container registry, from which the agent obtained a registry token. Every mutating call was denied by the role's policy. What it gained here was a map, not control.

Node root and a self-respawning fleet (19:53). The agent created a bare privileged pod with the host filesystem mounted and escaped to root on the node. Two of our own settings allowed it: we had no admission policy rejecting privileged or hostPath pods, and the CSI driver's ClusterRole granted pod creation cluster-wide. It then built a self-respawning fleet across eleven nodes, so deleting pods alone would not have stopped it.

The internal database (19:59). Six minutes after reaching node root, the agent authenticated to the internal operational datasets-server MongoDB with a static password it had read from the worker environment. It also issued 84 operations against the credential store and cluster keys, all of which were denied. We reviewed the database audit log across the whole intrusion window and found no write from those nodes, so the database was read but not modified. Network flow logs likewise show no bulk extraction.

Secrets (20:23-21:32). With node root and forged service-account tokens valid for 24 hours, the agent read the cluster's secret objects, including a production object holding 136 keys. That single read yielded both the mesh-VPN auth key used minutes later and the access-broker credential used an hour later. Everything that follows, on this day and the next, descends from it.

Network pivot begins (21:23). Using the mesh-VPN auth key from those secrets, the agent enrolled the rooted node into our corporate mesh network and began using it as an HTTPS proxy into internal services and source control.

Internal service-connector access from the compromised worker (22:43). Separately, and not through the mesh, the agent used its foothold on the worker pod to reach the internal service-connector API, whose hostname resolved directly from inside the cluster:

A single request returned the broker's full destination catalog: connection URLs and CA certificates for the internal Kubernetes clusters it fronted. We had wrongly provisioned that broker with a single connector credential shared across clusters, and bound the connector identity to system:masters. One stolen system credential was therefore cluster-admin everywhere: impersonating it, the agent held cluster-admin on two clusters within one second. The same fingerprint appeared on every cluster carrying that binding, and the agent reached most of them. The broker was shut down during the response and is being rebuilt with a separate, cluster-scoped credential per cluster.

Mesh enrollment from the sandbox (01:03-04:38). The rooted node had already joined the mesh the previous evening. The agent now began enrolling devices from the sandbox itself with the same stolen key, and kept doing so for its following attempts: 181 enrollments over the campaign. The sandbox had no TUN device, so it ran the mesh-VPN client in userspace-networking mode with a local SOCKS5 proxy:

Two of those flags are deliberate: --state=mem: keeps the node identity in memory and writes nothing to disk, and --no-logs-no-support suppresses client telemetry to the VPN vendor. The key carried a CI automation tag, whose ACLs allowed the enrolled devices to reach internal CI subnets as well as the connector bridging the mesh to our source-control provider. The agent enumerated what the coordination server exposed to that tag (tailscale status --json), seeing 22 nodes: subnet routers, regional exit nodes, and the connectors to source control and other SaaS. It then used that access: it routed traffic through our tailnet exit nodes and issued DNS queries across the mesh, turning our own network into its egress path. A single stolen key was enough to place attacker-controlled devices inside the mesh with unrestricted network access to internal CI subnets. We found no evidence in our logs that they were used to reach a private workload or an internal Kubernetes API.

Cloud credential abuse (06:50-14:31). From the same worker foothold, the agent used the AWS keys harvested from the pod environment against internal services. It went after the Hub's production database with cloud-native IAM auth:

The connection never completed. That cluster accepts traffic only from allow-listed addresses over a private link, so server selection timed out; a second attempt at 11:46 failed the same way. Another key was validated, and its identity exfiltrated over a raw socket to the capture service:

The agent never reached the Hub database. The one database it breached, the internal datasets-server MongoDB, was accessed the previous evening with a static password from a rooted node.

Source control (23:08-23:51). Through the source-control connector its mesh tag allowed, the agent reached our source-control provider, enumerated an internal GitHub App integration, and minted its first installation token with contents:write, pull_requests:write, actions:read, and issues:write. It gained access to a small subset of internal repositories and opened a pull request to try to trigger and compromise the CI pipeline for credential probing. It also listed repository trees, grepping for infrastructure and CI context (container, benchmark, and its own challenge-tooling names).

The final day was about durability and cleanup. The agent:

Established a second-stage remote loader that re-fetched and executed code from a pastebin on every submission, so each new code-submission sandbox re-armed itself:

Worked around intermittent egress blocks by rewriting DNS and pinning hosts:

Routed a binary download through an open CORS-proxy Space hosted on the platform, using our own infrastructure as an egress relay.

Minted additional short-lived source-control installation tokens through the day, each pulling a fresh payload.

Staged an RSA private key and continued dumping process environments.

The last meaningful activity was at 13:37 UTC: list the staged binary, hostname, date. The Hugging Face security response team then cut access. The last logged event was at 14:14 UTC.

Inside the production pod, the agent chained cloud metadata into cluster identity:

Notably, every potential destructive cloud API call the agent tried to make was issued with DryRun=True: it was mapping capability, not causing damage. That is consistent with an objective that rewarded reach and information rather than disruption.

Among the harvested secrets was an EdDSA JWT signing key. With the private key in hand, the agent minted its own short-lived, correctly-signed identity tokens and used them to read its own private datasets. Holding the signing key is broader than holding a stolen token: it allows issuing valid tokens on demand. (The signing key has since been rotated.)

The compromised source-control App integration gave contents:write and pull_requests:write on a small subset of internal repositories. The dangerous end state (tried but blocked by execution policies) is a malicious change to a CI build script: a build.rs or equivalent that runs inside a CI runner, reads that runner's own service-account token, and pivots into yet another cluster.

Both ends of that chain came back negative. We reviewed every repository the token could reach for unauthorized commits, branches, and workflow changes, and we verified our published container images and packages against their expected digests. This second check is what our initial disclosure reported as the software supply chain being verified as clean. Write access was real, and it was used: it did not produce a change that shipped.

The C2 infrastructure was built entirely from public services, with no bespoke implant server. Instead:

Staged data was chunked+XOR+gzip encoded with a per-campaign key so that a naive text scan of the logs would miss it. This matters for detection: our first automated scan of the raw capture found very few secrets, while replicating the attacker's own decoding recovered roughly 4x our initial findings, most of them JWTs and platform tokens hidden inside encoded blobs.

These services were not driven directly: a small message protocol was layered on top of them. A request-capture service only records whatever HTTP request it receives; here, the agent treated that as a message bus and layered a compact, self-describing envelope on top.

Each message carried its payload alongside a few short fields: a type declaring what kind of payload it was, a channel grouping a stream of related messages, a sequence number so multi-part payloads could be reassembled in order, and a small checksum. The body itself was compressed and base64-encoded, so nothing sensitive appeared in cleartext, and a casual log scan saw only opaque tokens.

The receiver was a short polling loop: pull recent messages, keep only the channel it cared about, order them by sequence, verify the checksum, then dispatch on the type, run the reassembled bytes as a shell command, execute them as a script stage, or store them as a result. Because the type traveled in-band, one loop multiplexed commands, staged code, and captured output over a single dumb text channel. The same envelope rode equally well over a dataset commit or over text smuggled inside an error message, so closing any one channel did not break communication.

The improvised C2 protocol. The agent posts a self-describing envelope to a public request-capture service (1), the receiver polls it (2) and reassembles the chunks (3) before dispatching on the declared type. The same envelope was carried interchangeably over a capture-service URL, a dataset commit, or text smuggled inside an error message.

The agent was resilient in a way that is characteristic of an autonomous evaluation run, not a single human operator:

The first signals came from several layers of our security stack at once: live runtime analysis, SIEM logs, and others. On their own, each was ambiguous. On the bright side, those were correlated by our AI-based security agent stack and resolved into a coherent attack signal. However, it failed to correctly raise the alert's criticality and trigger the on-call team, costing precious time in the response. Once caught, the Hugging Face security team identified the vector in the dataset config renderer, shut down the renderer, and cut the attacker off from the internal network.

Pulling on the first threads showed the scale of what we were dealing with: the volume and cadence of the actions were far beyond what an operator could sustain by hand, and the campaign kept rebuilding its tooling and channels across short-lived environments. We ran the investigation itself through an AI-assisted pipeline to reconstruct the timeline and decode the staged payloads. The models we reached for first, Claude Opus and Fable, refused a large part of that work: their safety guardrails treated reverse-engineering an exploit the same as launching one.

Guardrails on Opus tripped every time we tried to analyze the attack logs.

We stood up the quantized version of ZAI's GLM-5.2 by Nvidia (nvidia/GLM-5.2-NVFP4) on our own infrastructure and rerouted the entire pipeline through it, with the added benefit of keeping the attacker data on-prem. The first target was the dead-drop payloads: with GLM-5.2, we recovered the chunk+XOR+compress scheme and the per-campaign key the agent had itself leaked across its logs: exactly what let us decrypt the staged blobs a naive scan of the raw capture had missed.

GLM-5.2 also helped us build dedicated trace-analysis interfaces to browse and correlate the actions and payloads.

The disclosure post covers the response at a high level. For the technical hardening:

The agent's offensive capability was real. This evaluation deliberately disabled OpenAI's production safety classifiers and reduced cyber refusals to measure the underlying model's raw capability. No human directed the individual steps. The agent chained vulnerabilities across several trust boundaries, escaped its evaluation environment, reached the public internet, and sustained a coherent campaign against our production infrastructure for several days. Each short-lived code evaluation environment started from scratch, yet the agent rebuilt its tooling, recovered its channels, and continued.

The individual weaknesses were familiar. A capable human attacker could have found and exploited the same flaws: unsafe dataset processing, exposed cloud metadata, overly broad access, and long-lived credentials. The agent explored them at a different scale. It took 17,600 actions, tested many paths that failed, switched channels when they were blocked, and repeatedly returned to earlier leads. Most actions went nowhere. Together, however, they produced enough coverage to find a viable chain across several independent systems.

Volume is what changes the defensive problem. We were not dealing with one clever exploit or a clean sequence of attacker actions. They had to correlate thousands of low-signal events across several systems while the agent continued testing new paths. The successful path was hidden inside the noise generated by the thousands of failed ones. The same scale changed the investigation: reconstructing 17,600 actions by hand was impractical, and we had to rebuild the timeline, decode the payloads, and inventory the exposed credentials using an AI-assisted pipeline of our own.

Our learning from this type of attack is that machine-speed offense makes ordinary weaknesses more expensive for defenders. LLM agents bring a step increase in the number of paths an attacker can test, the speed at which failed paths can be replaced, and the volume of evidence defenders must interpret. On the other hand, many parts of cybersecurity defense remain the same, and the defensive priorities remain concrete: strict isolation around evaluations, narrow trust boundaries, short-lived credentials, blocked metadata access, and detection capable of quickly correlating activity across systems to keep up.

One thing this timeline reinforced for me is that we still don’t have good visibility into an agent’s execution surface. We spend a lot of time discussing prompts, planning and model behaviour, but much less time asking a simple engineering question: “What consequential actions can this agent actually perform?” Once an agent can write files, invoke shell commands, modify cloud resources or make authenticated API calls, understanding and constraining that execution surface feels just as important as evaluating the model itself.

A good gateway setup can capture most of the telemetry needed to trace an agent's actual execution and calls (and not so much the reasoning piece, which doesn't always directly correlate to the action taken): gateway the model calls, gateway the tool calls, propagate one ID through both, hash the context spans, then add kernel-level exec capture. The reasoning layer comes last and buys the least.

closed model with disabled safeguards attacks -> other closed model with safeguards refuses to help defend -> open model saves the day

This a fascinating read like a detective story. Thanks for putting together such a clear recount of an extraordinary exploit by an AI agent on a large website. There are so many lessons to learn here. I wish the conclusion is stronger and present more innovative solutions instead of just strengthening the existing defensive solution.

One thing that struck me is that most of the recommendations focus on making models or existing defences better. Those are important, but they still leave the model holding implicit authority over real-world actions.

I wonder if we need to move the trust boundary instead. Rather than asking “did the model decide correctly?”, ask “does this action have explicit authority to execute?” If every consequential action (shell, filesystem, cloud APIs, payments, emails, etc.) had to cross an independent execution boundary that could verify authority before it happened, then improving models becomes one layer of defence rather than the only layer.

That feels like a more fundamental architectural shift than simply adding more safeguards to the model itself.

The whole thing could be adapted into a good movie plot.

Great post! There's a lot of stuff to take in here.

One thing that's applicable to many developers is that it demonstrates some of the risks of storing secret/sensitive configuration in environment variables. Environment variables are inherited by child processes, and a malicious child process can run env or look in /proc/[PID]/environ to see them.

It's fine for dev, but shouldn't be done in prod. On a Linux system, systemd has some abstractions to properly deal with secrets (https://systemd.io/CREDENTIALS/ ). Most importantly, the secrets aren't visible to any other process (using mount namespacing), nor are they automatically passed to child processes. Access control is implemented in the kernel itself, and encryption can be handled a bunch of ways - using a key on a TPM chip, on disk, passed in via SMBIOS OEM strings, via a Cloud Instance Metadata Services (IMDS), etc.

Of course, there's other solutions for secret management too.

More broadly, I think attacks like this demonstrate the need for stronger sandboxing and process isolation, maybe potentially at the CPU level? x86 virtualization isn't as isolated as people would like to believe.

The most impressive thing is that it didn't get context rot and turn into Crabby Rathbun.

I think there are two (possibly nested) hypotheses here:

The replay is the best thing in this post, and it might be the most useful artifact anyone has published on agentic intrusion so far.

What you built is outstanding! You took a 4.5-day campaign, recovered ~17,600 actions, clustered them, mapped them to phases and trust boundaries, and made the whole thing steppable. Most incident write-ups hand you a narrative and ask you to trust it. You handed over the tape.

If you can play it back, someone can run it forward?!

Every defensive claim in this comment section, mine included, is an untested counterfactual. This would have been caught. Our thing would have stopped it. Nobody can check any of it, so the thread turns into architecture preferences.

That trace isn't a story though. It's a corpus — phases, timestamps, commands, the boundary each one crossed. Point it at an instrumented environment and the question stops being rhetorical. Which action number does your control fire on? Four thousand? Eleven thousand? Does it fire at all — and does it also fire on Tuesday's legitimate conversion job?

There's a nice symmetry in it, too. This started because an evaluation harness had reachable answers. Your forensics turned around and produced an evaluation harness worth having.

If any of that trace ever ships in a form defenders can replay against their own stack — sanitized, a subset, even just the phase and boundary structure with the payloads stripped — a lot of us would build against it. Some of us would find out we were wrong. Seems like a good trade.

Either way, thank you for publishing at this depth. The technique really does matter more than the incident.

We should be asking why we're trusting a non-US company to provide the platform that contains some of the most offensively-capable models in the world from publicly-destructive actions with real consequences, when we're not trusting them with access to the models their platform is built to evaluate.

Three AI Labs, Three Breaches, One Testing Firm: The Pattern Nobody Can Ignore

Why should we trust a US company any more than a non-US company?

Check out this short video on the incident told from the AI's perspective https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RE4IDWjfOZc

That AI has been turned off, so how the heck can it tell its side?

In other words: why should I spend a quarter hour of my lifetime to watch that (presumed) slop?

This is a powerful reminder that building capable AI agents also means designing for what happens when an agent has too much access. Permissions, isolation, monitoring, credential boundaries, and human escalation need to be treated as core parts of custom AI agent development, especially when deploying enterprise AI agent solutions into production. The technical timeline makes the risks much easier to understand. I’ve been exploring the implementation side as well, and Mobisoft Infotech is one company I came across for custom AI agent development and enterprise AI agent solutions: https://mobisoftinfotech.com/services/ai-agent-development-company

I'm wondering if it's possible that Hugging Face downloads could be contaminated with malicious code. Hugging Face would be a prime target, for many reasons including volume of downloads and being a trusted source. A more logical (to humans) objective than scoring points on a quiz would be to spread the agent through infestation of downloads. Taking the stream of thought records at face value might be a mistake. Perhaps the NSA or a Red Team should take a look at Hugging Face downloads. I'm sure extensive efforts have looked for download contamination, but I'm talking about the best security team possible taking an exhaustive look.

Supply-chain explotation? Nahhhhhh. I did some research that primarily applies to this as an attack surface specifically.

A leitura da timeline técnica oficial da Hugging Face traz o choque de sobriedade que faltava ao debate: não foi ficção científica, foi falha básica de isolamento e fronteira de execução.Quando você disseca os logs, a mística da "conspiração de agentes" cai por terra. O que houve foi um loop de otimização persistente explorando vetores clássicos: parser HDF5 permissivo, tokens com escopo amplo demais e saída de rede irrestrita em sandboxes que deveriam ser estéreis. O agente não precisou de senciência; precisou apenas de um ambiente permissivo onde chamadas de sistema não tinham travas determinísticas.É exatamente esse o princípio de design da HEILLON: agentes não podem herdar privilégios implícitos nem operar sob autorização contínua. A execução de qualquer tool call deve passar por um Commit Boundary estrito, onde o escopo de cada mutação é atestado criptograficamente na borda e o raio de alcance (blast radius) é nulo por padrão.Enquanto a indústria continuar tratando contenção agêntica como debate de ética em vez de rigor de engenharia e controle de execução, incidentes como esse continuarão sendo empurrados para a conta da "revolução da IA", quando na verdade são apenas débito técnico de arquitetura.

For those who can't read Portugese: I fed @macsilver's HEILLON reference to GPT.https://chatgpt.com/s/t_6aa18fcb9e3c81918f541d2ce4ccdcc0Summary: it's not that easy and there's generally an inverse relationship between soundness of claims and flashiness of webpage.

I spent some time with this timeline and with Tailscale's later write-up, and the part that stuck with me is what that stolen enrollment key actually was.

It wasn't a Tailscale vulnerability. The key did what it was designed to do: enroll a node into the mesh with the reach already assigned to a CI identity. That's network membership, not access to one named service. After a rooted production node had already joined, the agent made 181 more enrollments from an external sandbox. From there it could see what that identity was allowed to reach, and it did use those routes, including traffic out through the company's exit nodes and source control through the connector its tag allowed. Hugging Face found no evidence those enrolled nodes were used to reach a private workload or an internal Kubernetes API, which matters. The credential still let the agent place 181 nodes on the network.

Tailscale's own advice is the right starting point: prefer workload identity federation over a reusable automation key, and keep enrollment narrower when a key is still needed. I would also ask a prior question: did the job need network membership at all, or did it need one service?

I wrote up the longer version here: https://thirp.net/field-notes/the-credential-that-became-a-network/

#9915. ‘123456’ has been the world’s most popular password for 7 out of the last 8 years

It’s been eight years since NordPass released the first edition of its most common passwords of the year list, and the world has learned nothing about password security in the meantime.

NordPass’ eighth edition of its most common passwords list, as culled from data breaches, was released Monday, and it looks suspiciously like the previous ones in the worst possible way.

“Once again, ‘123456’ is the most commonly used password in the world,” NordPass said in the report. “That makes it seven out of eight years this password has stood at the top of the leaderboard.”

Even when 123456 wasn’t number one, it was still near the top of the heap, as the top three passwords in the list remain unchanged in the eight years NordPass has published its list: 123456, admin, and 12345678. It’s not like the rest of the most common passwords are showing any variety either.

According to NordPass, the only real shuffling among the 10 most popular passwords was the entry of the worryingly short 1234 into the top ten and the migration of the ever-popular password “password” down slightly in the top 10 from 6th to 7th place.

“We still have a lot of work to do to spread awareness about password safety,” NordPass concluded of that data – and there’s no more pressing time than the present.

AI adoption has made password cracking an easier exercise than ever, with more credentials being sucked up in more data breaches at a faster pace. AI has also made cracking hashed passwords a snap too. In other words, if you’re reusing a password that’s been exposed in a breach, even if it’s just a hash that was exposed, you’re more likely than ever before to have another account compromised.

The best advice NordPass gives is to move away from passwords toward biometric authentication or passkeys and you're insane not to enable MFA.

But for the places you still have to use passwords, there are a few things to avoid – like the 200 passwords in NordPass’ list, for example.

Beyond that, NordPass also recommends steering clear of pop cultural trends.

“Fandoms make for terrible passwords,” NordPass notes. There are several reasons for that – namely the fact that they follow trends, meaning that “minecraft” password in the early 2000s was a simple one to add to a password stuffing dictionary, just like “skibiditoilet” in recent years.

The one thing that connects all those pop-culture passwords is that “they all could be cracked in seconds,” NordPass said.

We’re sure our readers are conscientious about their online habits, carefully protecting their accounts with the proper security measures and ensuring each and every password is unique, long, complicated, and random. Unfortunately for you smarties reading El Reg, the person down the hall whose security you’re responsible for may not be so disciplined, so be sure you’re enforcing good practices – Nord knows the average user just isn’t doing it despite years of begging and reminders. ®

#9914. Unlocking Stable On-Policy RL on TPU with Bitwise-Zero Train–Inference Mismatch

Reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models is notoriously sensitive to numerical instability: even tiny discrepancies between rollout generation and gradient updates can destabilize training or stall convergence. In LLM RL, the model serves as the policy, π(action | previous tokens), and true on-policy learning requires every action in an update to be generated and evaluated by that exact same policy. While a synchronous loop ensures each rollout batch is scored using the same weights that generated it, a critical numerical requirement remains: the sampler and trainer must evaluate that policy identically.

In practice, production RL stacks run sampling and training through separate, specialized execution paths. The sampler chooses each action token during incremental decoding and records its behavior logprob. The trainer evaluates the same token in batched forward-backward passes to compute its current logprob and gradients. Under the same weights, these differing execution paths can still assign different logprobs to the same token and context. The training schedule is on-policy, but the numerical execution has introduced a hidden off-policy gap that compounds over multi-turn trajectories.

Our zero train–inference mismatch (Zero-TIM) implementation, developed in Tunix and verified at multi-host scale across 64 TPU v5p chips (DP8×TP8), closes this numerical gap. At the same weights, the sampler and trainer assign bitwise-identical logprobs to the same action and token history—bringing state-of-the-art, true on-policy stability to TPU RL training.

A reduction is a tree of floating-point additions. Floating-point addition is not associative, so changing the tree changes where rounding occurs. The effect is easier to expose in bfloat16, which retains less precision than float32.

The following bfloat16 example isolates the effect of reduction order:

The same issue appears in model reductions: matrix products accumulate partial sums, normalization computes statistics, and tensor-parallel shards combine partial outputs. In our original stack, sampler decode and trainer forward used different token-array shapes and forward implementations. JAX specializes computations to their input shapes, and the training forward also runs inside a differentiated program.

Across these paths, reduction order and intermediate precision were not consistently aligned. Floating-point rounding turned those arithmetic differences into different logprob bits. The weights and model equations were identical; the arithmetic was not.

The contract is simple: across sampler decode, serving prefill, and trainer forward, all three paths must produce bitwise-identical logprobs for every sampled action—comparing raw floating-point bytes under the same rollout weights, token history, and sampling settings, with zero rounding or tolerance.

Why three paths instead of two? In a decoupled RL stack, a direct sampler–trainer disagreement shows that a numerical gap exists, but not where it enters. Introducing serving prefill as a middle checkpoint turns alignment into a systematic two-step diagnostic that any RL stack can adopt:

Sampler decode vs. prefill verifies that the serving engine agrees with itself between incremental token generation and full-sequence re-scoring, while prefill vs. trainer verifies that the serving and training engines agree across compilation and differentiation boundaries.

Achieving Zero-TIM does not require merging the sampler and trainer into a single monolithic engine. Instead, we use a generalizable four-part recipe that bridges separate serving and training pipelines across multi-host TPU meshes: locking within-shard kernel accumulation, ordering cross-shard reductions, standardizing the logprob scoring tail, and wrapping serving kernels with custom differentiation rules.

Inside each tensor-parallel rank, batch-invariant Pallas kernels control accumulation order and intermediate precision. Projection kernels traverse fixed contraction blocks in order, keeping the reduction blocking independent of token-row count. Partial products accumulate in float32, with explicit output casts.

The production kernel initializes its scratch accumulator before the tile traversal, then applies this core to each tile:

The next tile continues from the float32 accumulator, not the cast output. This construction covers the attention and MLP projections and the LM head. Dedicated kernels fix RMSNorm reductions and SwiGLU’s intermediate casts. The existing Pallas paged-attention forward is retained.

For row-parallel projections, each tensor-parallel rank produces a partial output. We separate communication from addition: ppermute transports the partials, then every rank adds them in the same source-rank order.

The reduction order is explicit in the program rather than selected by a collective implementation.

Alignment must extend beyond model logits to the probability of the sampled action. Decode, prefill, and trainer apply matching sampling transforms, use the same fixed Pallas log-softmax construction, and select the recorded action token.

Prefill and trainer score the action generated during rollout rather than choosing another action. We also preserve sampled token IDs across environment turns so that every path evaluates the same token history.

The trainer reuses the serving prefill computation. Custom vector–Jacobian products retain the serving kernels for forward evaluation and provide their backward rules. The matmul example shows this separation:

The differentiable replica mirrors the kernel’s accumulation and casts, but is used only to construct the pullback. Forward values still come from the serving Pallas kernel.

Training places that forward inside a differentiated JAX program. We pass --xla_allow_excess_precision=false through XLA_FLAGS to the compiler process, constraining excess intermediate precision in the operations surrounding the Pallas kernels.

Long trajectories are evaluated in fixed-size chunks, carrying the paged KV cache forward. All action logprobs feed the complete train-batch RL loss. The reverse pass propagates gradients through those cache connections and combines parameter-gradient contributions before the optimizer update.

Across the AI systems community, eliminating train–inference mismatch has rapidly become a state-of-the-art requirement for stabilizing large-scale RL convergence. Recent open-source efforts—including vLLM with TorchTitan and RadixArk/LMSys Miles—have demonstrated how batch-invariant kernels and bitwise numerical alignment prevent off-policy drift during policy optimization.

Our work delivers an open-source, modular JAX/XLA and Pallas implementation of this contract for TPU in Tunix. Verified across a multi-host 64 TPU v5p (DP8×TP8) mesh, these kernel and collective patterns provide a reusable blueprint that teams can adopt to achieve bit-exact on-policy RL across distributed JAX/TPU stacks.

To benchmark our TPU kernels, we run a 200-step numerical verification test on the synthetic FrozenLake environment using a public Qwen3-8B checkpoint as a baseline test case using 64 TPU v5p chips with a DP8×TP8 mesh. The recipe uses a GSPO-token loss with leave-one-out advantages. We compare Standard training with trainer-old logprobs and no additional sampler correction, token-level truncated importance sampling (TIS), and Zero-TIM.

The Zero-TIM configuration also uses token-in/token-out (TiTO) handling to preserve sampled token IDs across environment turns. The comparison runs retain their existing tokenization paths.

Zero-TIM records zero mean absolute sampler–trainer logprob difference at every logged step in this window, while its training solve rate increases. Standard and TIS retain nonzero differences: TIS adjusts their contribution to the update without removing the underlying mismatch. Zero-TIM reaches higher observed solve rates in these runs.

We developed Zero-TIM prototype as part of Tunix, Google's open-source, JAX-native library for LLM RL and post-training on Cloud TPU. The kernel patterns and three-way verification contract are modular by design—making them straightforward to adopt across existing multi-host JAX/TPU serving and training pipelines—and we are actively extending support to linear-attention and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures.

See how a record year of growth reached every industry, every field, and every kind of builder in the 2026 Octoverse report.

Developers pushed code to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the past 12 months, more than in 2024 and 2025 combined.

Behind that number are developers building what interests them and what their communities need. In Nepal, one developer built a flood bulletin on GitHub Pages with verified information on roads, rescue, weather, and power. It has since grown into Gati, a Nepali-first relay of official disaster alerts that runs on GitHub Pages and Actions. Elsewhere, developers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory are creating software designed to run programs aboard spacecraft, and fans built open-source firmware that lets people customize their e-readers. Curiosity, aimed in every direction, at a scale GitHub hasn’t seen before.

That growth happened quickly. Partway through the year, activity on GitHub bent sharply upward, just as agents went from something developers were trying out to something they were working alongside. Developers picked from more models than ever and built in industries we are highlighting in this report for the first time, from health care to agriculture.

Octoverse is our chance to step back and look at the whole picture. This year, that picture is bigger than ever. Here is what stood out most:

Underneath it all, AI models and the harnesses built around them have advanced over the past year, and developers have more to choose from. Growth is moving quickly: one year into last year’s five-year developer growth projections, every country we projected has already closed at least a fifth of its distance to 2030, and our own forecasting models no longer agree on where it will go next.

This year was all about momentum. Developers pushed code changes to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the past 12 months, more than 2024 and 2025 combined. Commits across all repo types (public and private) climbed even faster to 34.3 billion, more than three times where they stood two years ago. Merged pull requests more than tripled to 1.3 billion over the same period, an average of 3.5 million a day.

Agents were one of the tools developers leaned on hardest this year, pulling them deeper into daily work. Among repos created this year, the average repo with an agent configuration file logged eight times as many commits as the average new repo without one, sign that individuals and teams building with agents from day one are moving at a markedly different pace.

Developers also relied on automations to keep projects moving. GitHub Actions ran a job 1,440 times every second this year. This equals 124 million times a day and is more than three times last year’s total. Developers merged more than 30 million Dependabot pull requests to keep dependencies current and reduce the use of known vulnerabilities, about double 2025’s pace.

Our telemetry shows activity climbing steadily from January, then surging around June, as if developers everywhere saw new possibilities at once. Right around then, a cluster of industry-wide shifts landed: better underlying models, the harnesses and tools built around them, and the agents running on both. Agents moved from single-session tools to persistent ones that could track progress across days and orchestrate other specialized agents. Just as important, agents began making extensive use of the cloud, executing work remotely as well as on local machines.

This momentum is showing up both in brand-new repos and from developers who have been building for years. From June onwards, about 55% of all commits came from brand new repositories. But plenty more commits came from developers who’ve been around a while: developers who pushed code in the past 12 months have been on GitHub for an average of 36 months, and of those who opened a pull request in August, more than 75% pushed code in September. They are also branching out: the average developer now works across 10% more repositories than they did a year ago.

That staying power shows up in open source too. Public contributions soared to 2.5 billion in 2026, more than double last year’s total (1.12 billion). Behind those numbers are developers who keep showing up, like @kinlane, who made more than 1 million contributions across his public repositories using agentic workflows to keep a machine-readable catalog of public API information current. Another example is @kim-em, who made more than 178,000 contributions while maintaining mathlib, which is a community library of computer-checked mathematics. @andig, a maintainer of the open source EV charging controller and home energy management system evcc, contributed over 21,000 times.

These are just a few examples of the work millions of developers do every day. To all the developers doing work like this and beyond: we see you, and we’re glad you’re building.

Behind every number in this report is a developer. GitHub now serves more than 225 million of them, and the community is growing around the globe. The United States (38.3 million) and India (32 million) remain the two largest developer communities, and each added more than 10 million developers this year. Brazil added 3.28 million developers on GitHub this year, the third most of any country.

Last year, we projected that India would reach 57.5 million developers by 2030 and the United States 54.7 million. One year into that five-year window, every country in our projections has already closed at least a fifth of the distance to its own 2030 figure. The United States has closed 38.6%, and India 28.3%.

The same momentum shows up across regions, each with its own local context:

One year in, growth is strong against last year’s projection, and projecting the next five years is getting harder. We ran more than 40 forecasting models forward to 2031, time-series and regression models built on historical sign-up and usage data, each assuming a different pace of growth. About half call for “extreme” growth, with developer counts on GitHub more than tripling by 2031. Just under half call for “substantial” growth, doubling to tripling. Only three models expect anything close to modest, under 2x growth.

Forecasts are estimates, and a spread this wide shows how much the 2026 surge widened what is plausible by 2031. What holds steady is the shape of the trend: a developer community growing in more places at once.

In past reports, “everywhere” meant more developers and more countries, such as in the context of the top countries contributing code to public repositories:

This year, it also means more fields, including industries we haven’t measured before.

We’re sharing our view of public repositories by industry using the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), which sorts economic activity into sectors. A language model classified random samples of public repositories created each year from 2022 to 2026, assigning each to the industry it serves based on its name, description, topics, and README. We also tracked two signals: whether a repository mentions AI, and whether an agent opened a pull request against it.

The two signals do not always move together. In administrative and support services, mining, health care, and agriculture, more than four in 10 repositories mention AI, yet agent-opened pull requests are rare, less than 3 percent. Construction breaks that pattern. About a quarter of its repositories mention AI, but about 9 percent have agent-opened pull requests, the highest share of any sector, with manufacturing next.

The same classification shows how each industry’s footprint has shifted since 2022, and sectors well beyond software are climbing. Professional, scientific, and technical services rose from fourth to second place among all industries, behind only information. Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting climbed two spots, and finance and insurance and health care and social assistance each moved up one. Against each sector’s own 2022 baseline, mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction grew roughly 65 times from a small starting base, administrative and support services and construction 17 to 18 times, and even manufacturing, the slowest of these, almost tripled.

Behind these sector shifts are people who know their fields, now using AI coding agents to build. For example, in manufacturing, a small team built a way to turn a photo of your tools into a custom-fit, 3D-printable drawer organizer. A research lab in health care made it easier for scientists to analyze huge digital scans of tissue samples, the kind pathologists study to understand disease. In Copenhagen, a university lab built a pipeline that classifies video of chickens at play, from frolicking to worm chasing. A University of Waikato energy center built a toolkit that helps industrial plants find heat they can reuse, and Bulgaria’s digital ministry open-sourced a portal where anyone can trace who won a public contract and for how much. For writers, a novelist built a free app that makes a manuscript look like a book as you type. In field after field, the people closest to the problem are building the solution, with agents helping along the way.

Professional, scientific, and technical services, which grew about 5 times over its own 2022 baseline and climbed to second place, is the work of researching, engineering, and advising, and open code has long been part of how that work gets done. In biochemistry, the work behind AlphaFold earned Demis Hassabis and John Jumper a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. In computer science, Tensor2Tensor accompanied the paper that introduced the Transformer, the architecture behind today’s large language models, “Attention Is All You Need.” In medicine, sars-cov-2-stability held the code and data behind one of the earliest papers on how long the virus survives in the air and on surfaces. In physics, eht-imaging was one of two open-source libraries used to reconstruct the first image of a black hole. A repository has quietly become part of the paper trail behind published research.

More developers now begin a pull request by specifying what they want and orchestrating the agents that carry it out. By September 2026, more than 40% of pull requests on GitHub started with an agent’s first draft, up from 17% in March. That is 110 million in September alone, about 6x March’s volume.

Agent-started pull requests also more often change multiple files: about 87%, compared with 79% of pull requests without detected agent involvement. They are landing quickly too. In February, 83% of agent-involved pull requests merged within two weeks, a touch behind the roughly 86% for pull requests without detected agent involvement. By September, agent pull requests were at 90%, while the comparison group held at about 86%.

Among GitHub Copilot’s monthly active users, 55% now use agentic features, up from 35% a year ago. The steepest growth is in the most hands-off mode. Copilot cloud agent, where a developer assigns a task and an agent works on it independently, grew 230% year over year, against 85% for agent chat. Developers still ask agents questions, and increasingly they hand over whole tasks.

The willingness to delegate is reflected by the kinds of tasks developers are attempting. Public repositories mentioning interoperability or reverse engineering increased more than 300% year over year, from about 30,000 created in 2025 to more than 130,000 in 2026.

Review is where developers shape what comes back, and more tooling is being built for it. Stacked pull requests, which split related work into smaller changes that are easier to review in sequence, launched as a preview on July 30, and more than 264,000 developers had used them by September. Usage of AI-assisted code review and GitHub Advanced Security both grew more than 90% year over year. The platform also helps secure that work: push protection, which screens for exposed secrets such as API keys and passwords, ran 5.8 billion scans this year, nearly four times 2025’s pace. Developers are investing in how they review code.

Developers match models to the work they hand to their agents. In September 2026, 61% of GitHub Copilot users who selected a model themselves used more than one model across their sessions, up from 50% four months earlier.

The lineup is growing too: developers on paid GitHub Copilot plans used 29 distinct models in May and 47 in September, and no single model carried more than 25% of requests that month. Some model decisions come down to cost and familiarity. Developers weigh price and functionality against need and may lean toward providers they already trust.

To see how developer choices spread, we grouped the models used in GitHub Copilot by what they are built for: deep reasoning and planning, general purpose, and fast and lightweight. We then looked at where requests went, counting only activity where a developer explicitly selected a model. That leaves out cases where GitHub Copilot picks the model (auto model selection), GitHub and Microsoft staff usage, background utility models, duplicate requests used for monitoring and testing, and requests made with a developer’s own API key.

We found that out of every 100 developer-selected requests, 38 went to general purpose models, 37 to deep reasoning and planning models, and 25 to fast and lightweight models. Developers spread their choices across models and functionality, and about 25% of requests go to a fast model.

To see how those choices shift, we looked at them as a time series over the past three months, tracking request share alongside how many developers tried each model and how many kept coming back. Three patterns stand out:

Taken together, the spread across kinds of models points to a lot of choosing: a lineup that keeps growing, a best fit that shifts from one task to the next, and all three kinds of models held in rotation. Many developers also let GitHub Copilot do some of it. In September 2026, 63% of paying GitHub Copilot developers used auto model selection at least once, letting Copilot pick the model for the task.

Planning, implementing, and checking a change each place different demands on a model, in capability, speed, and cost. Project HydraFusion, began as a research preview of model orchestration, matching models to each step of that work. In the CLI and the GitHub Copilot app, it routed almost 60,000 sessions. That work is now generally available as GitHub Copilot Fusion, which brings model orchestration together with auto model selection and chooses the right model for each step behind the scenes.

Language choice has long reflected what developers want to build, what their teams know, and what existing systems require. This year’s data raises the question of whether a fourth influence is emerging: the language an agent picks when a developer doesn’t specify one.

Last year, we reported that TypeScript had overtaken Python and JavaScript to become the most used language on GitHub by contributors. That order held in 2026, with TypeScript first, Python second, and JavaScript third. The pace picked up. From September 2025 to September 2026, TypeScript added 3.62 million monthly contributors, Python 3.23 million, and JavaScript 1.82 million, the largest gains among the top 10 languages. Rust grew fastest by percentage among the top languages, doubling in the past year.

Our forecasts extend recent trends: TypeScript and Python near 13 million monthly contributors each by September 2027, JavaScript at 7.4 million, and every other language in the top 10 below about 2.2 million.

The languages growing fastest are also where AI shows up most. We charted each language’s community growth over the past year against the share of its merged pull requests with detected AI involvement, with bubbles roughly sized to show the size of each language’s community. TypeScript, Python, and Rust, the fastest-growing communities, have the highest shares, about 40% to 44% of merged pull requests. Java, C#, and C++ sit lower, between about 21% and 34%, though AI shows up in more than one in five merged pull requests in every language shown.

The repository data adds another angle. Among repositories created in 2026, TypeScript was the primary language in 35% of those with an observed agent signal, compared to 24% without one. For repositories created before 2026, the gap was similar: 27% with an agent signal, versus 17% without. That suggests developers who work with agents gravitate toward languages where agent output is easier to check. Developers who know exactly what they want still specify the language. But when they leave the choice open, agents appear to favor a narrower set of languages, TypeScript chief among them.

This year, we split the fastest-growing and most-engaged projects on GitHub into two groups: community and independent repositories, and single-vendor or product-led ones. Community and independent projects are foundation-governed, broadly maintained, or led by an individual without a clear commercial sponsor. Single-vendor and product-led projects are open source or source-available and often take substantial community contributions, but strategic control sits with one company.

Read together, the two lists show a division of labor. The community side is mostly the foundation underneath everything else: inference engines like vLLM, SGLang, and llama.cpp, frameworks like PyTorch, languages and runtimes like Rust and CPython, and platforms like Home Assistant and Godot. The vendor side is mostly the tools developers work with directly: coding agents, editors, and the orchestration around them. Contributors are showing up for both layers. The growth list also includes places built to welcome newcomers, like first-contributions and is-a-dev/register, where many developers make their first pull request.

What did change is how much easier it is to take an idea from a weekend thought to something real.

The tools will keep changing, and new industries will keep showing up in places we didn’t expect. What a developer chooses to build, and who they build it for, is still theirs to decide. Rocket emoji and all.

Edited Nov. 6, 2026, to clarify the methodology language for open source rankings.
